MCQoriginal-hard-u3-taxation-02

A student writes in an essay: 'The petitions of the Stamp Act Congress in 1765 prove that the colonists were already committed to independence that year.' Which of the following best evaluates this claim?

  1. A is supported, because the street actions of the Sons of Liberty -- burning stamps and hanging tax collectors in effigy -- show the colonies as a whole had turned toward independence
  2. B is supported, because independence came only eleven years later, which shows the 1765 petitions were the first step toward separation
  3. C is undermined, because the petitions were written in polite and formal language, which shows the colonists were not deeply upset with Parliament
  4. D is undermined, because the petitions professed loyalty to the king and demanded the rights of English subjects within the empire rather than separation from it
Answer and explanation

Key: D

The 1765 petitions professed loyalty to the king and demanded the rights of English subjects within the empire; the turn toward independence came later, after further conflicts. Reading later independence back into 1765, generalizing from militants to the whole population, or treating the petitions' formal tone as proof of mild feeling all miss what the petitions actually said.

  • A: Wrong. The militant actions of the Sons of Liberty do not show what the whole colonial population wanted -- and fierce protest against a tax is not the same as a commitment to independence.
  • B: Wrong. That independence came eleven years later does not prove the 1765 petitions began the drive for it; a later outcome cannot supply an earlier intent.
  • C: Wrong. Petitions are written in formal language as a matter of genre; the tone of the document is not a measure of how seriously the petitioners pressed their constitutional claims.
  • D: Right. The petitions' language of loyalty and rights within the empire contradicts the claim of an existing commitment to independence.

Pennsylvania's 1780 law for the gradual abolition of slavery declared children born to enslaved mothers after its passage free upon reaching age twenty-eight, while people already enslaved remained enslaved for life.

A student argues that the American Revolution ended slavery in Pennsylvania. Which consideration best qualifies this claim?

  1. A The law freed no one immediately: those already enslaved stayed enslaved for life, and their children still owed decades of labor — the Revolution started a slow process, not an ending.
  2. B The law proves that revolutionary ideals changed nothing at all about slavery anywhere in America, in the North or the South, in 1780 or in any later year.
  3. C The law shows that Pennsylvania's leaders rejected the Revolution's ideals.
  4. D The law was caused only by Quaker religious beliefs and had nothing to do with the Revolution, its ideals, the wartime service of Black soldiers, or the changing economic interests of Pennsylvania.
Answer and explanation

Key: A

Qualifying means adding what the simple story leaves out. The 1780 act was real progress — the first such law in America — but 'ended slavery' overstates it badly: a person enslaved in 1779 died enslaved. Revolutionary ideals helped make the law possible, Quaker activism pushed it, and economic and political interests watered it down. The honest claim is that the Revolution began slavery's slow retreat in the North, not that it finished the job.

  • A: Correct. The law's own terms — no immediate freedom, lifetime bondage for those already enslaved, decades of labor owed by their children — qualify the student's claim into a more accurate one about gradual change.
  • B: This overcorrects. The law was a genuine, ideals-driven breakthrough and a model for other northern states; saying the Revolution changed nothing ignores the gradual abolition movement it helped start.
  • C: The law's supporters invoked the Revolution's ideals of liberty; gradualism reflected political and economic compromise with slaveholding interests, not rejection of the ideals.
  • D: Quaker activism mattered, but single-cause explanations fail here: revolutionary rhetoric, wartime service by Black soldiers, and economic calculation all shaped the law. 'Only' is the giveaway.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u3-migration-07
The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 prohibited slavery in the territory northwest of the Ohio River.

A historian calls the Ordinance 'the first federal law against slavery.' Which evidence most complicates that description?

  1. A The Ordinance alone created the Northwest as free territory, so this one federal law was the single decisive force behind the region's development.
  2. B The Ordinance's own fugitive provision treated escapees as property to be returned, and long-term indentures kept bound Black labor in the region for decades.
  3. C The Ordinance proves the founding generation was united in opposing slavery, sharing one antislavery purpose, one program, and one timetable for bringing it to an end.
  4. D The Ordinance had no real effect because western settlers simply ignored the ban entirely, holding enslaved people openly without consequence -- making the famous prohibition a dead letter from the start.
Answer and explanation

Key: B

Calling the Ordinance simply 'antislavery' leaves out what the law itself did for slavery: its fugitive clause ordered the return of escapees as property, and settlers used long-term indentures to keep bound Black labor in the region anyway. A ban with built-in protections for slaveholders needs a qualifier, not a slogan. (A) overcredits one law -- the region's free-labor future also depended on settlers, migration, and economics. (C) imagines a united founding generation that did not exist; the same era's Constitution protected the slave trade until 1808. (D) goes too far the other way: the ban genuinely shaped how the Northwest developed.

  • A: Wrong. This gives one statute the whole credit. The Northwest's development as free territory also depended on who settled there, migration patterns, and economics -- not on a single law alone.
  • B: Correct. The fugitive provision and the persistence of bound Black labor through indentures show that the anti-slavery ban coexisted with concrete protections for slavery -- the evidence that complicates the simple label.
  • C: Wrong. The same generation wrote a Constitution that barred Congress from touching the slave trade until 1808. The Ordinance reflects a divided, compromising generation, not a united one.
  • D: Wrong. The ban had real consequences: it shaped the Northwest's development as free territory. Loopholes weakened it, but 'no real effect' ignores how the region actually developed.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u3-philosophy-03
Source 1 -- A 1774 colonial pamphlet argues that a Parliament in which the colonies have no representatives cannot justly tax them, since government rests on the consent of the governed and a people may resist rulers who violate their natural rights. Source 2 -- A 1775 Loyalist pamphlet replies that colonists already enjoy the full rights of Englishmen because Parliament represents the whole empire, and that resisting lawful taxes is rebellion against that constitution.

Which statement best describes the relationship between the two arguments?

  1. A The colonial pamphlet invents a brand-new philosophy of rights out of nothing, while the Loyalist pamphlet simply defends obeying whatever Parliament decrees.
  2. B Both pamphlets argue from the same English constitutional tradition, but they disagree about how its principles apply to the colonies' situation.
  3. C The Loyalist pamphlet shows that Loyalists opposed liberty itself and wanted the colonies ruled as conquered subjects with no rights at all.
  4. D The two pamphlets agree on every important principle and differ only on small details of tax policy, so the whole crisis was basically a misunderstanding.
Answer and explanation

Key: B

Both pamphlets speak the same constitutional language -- consent, natural rights, the rights of Englishmen -- and use it to reach opposite conclusions about Parliament's power. The fight is over what those shared principles require in the colonies' case, not over whether liberty matters. (A) gets the history backwards: nobody here invents a philosophy from scratch, and the Loyalist is arguing constitutional law, not blind obedience. (C) caricatures Loyalists as enemies of liberty; Source 2 shows the Loyalist insisting colonists already possess English rights. (D) shrinks a genuine dispute over consent and representation into a mere misunderstanding.

  • A: Wrong. Neither pamphlet invents a philosophy from nothing, and the Loyalist is making a constitutional argument about representation, not preaching blind obedience to whatever Parliament decrees.
  • B: Correct. Both sources appeal to the same tradition -- English constitutionalism and natural rights -- and reach opposite conclusions because they disagree about how its principles apply to the colonies' situation.
  • C: Wrong. This caricatures Loyalists as opponents of liberty itself. Source 2 shows the Loyalist claiming colonists already enjoy the rights of Englishmen; the dispute is over what those rights require, not whether liberty matters.
  • D: Wrong. The sources show a real dispute over consent and representation, not a trivial mix-up. Disagreeing about the application of a principle is still disagreeing about something important.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u3-ratification-06
In a 1787 Anti-Federalist essay, 'Brutus' warns that the Constitution's necessary and proper clause will let Congress claim unlimited power, sweeping away every right the states have reserved.

Which statement best evaluates Brutus's warning as historical evidence?

  1. A It proves that the framers intended Congress to exercise unlimited power under the clause, sweeping aside every limit the Constitution appears to set.
  2. B It is confirmed because the federal government later used the clause to justify broad powers, which proves Brutus correctly grasped the framers' true and original design from the very start.
  3. C It is evidence of Anti-Federalist fears and persuasion tactics during ratification — Brutus wrote to defeat ratification, so his alarming reading must be weighed against Federalist replies.
  4. D It shows the Anti-Federalists opposed the Constitution because they actually favored monarchy and wanted a king ruling America rather than any republican government at all.
Answer and explanation

Key: C

Brutus was campaigning, not summarizing. His job was to frighten readers into rejecting the Constitution, so he read the clause in the most alarming way possible. That makes the essay excellent evidence of what Anti-Federalists feared and how they argued — and poor evidence of what the clause 'really meant,' a question the Federalists answered very differently and the courts took decades to settle.

  • A: This mistakes a critic's worst-case reading for the authors' intent. Brutus opposed the Constitution; his alarm about the clause tells us about his fears, not about what the framers meant to authorize.
  • B: What later generations did with the clause — McCulloch v. Maryland came in 1819 — cannot confirm what anyone intended in 1787. Later use is a different historical question from original meaning.
  • C: Correct. Sourcing asks what a document can and cannot show: Brutus's purpose (defeat ratification) and audience (wavering voters) make his essay strong evidence of Anti-Federalist argument and weak evidence of the clause's settled legal meaning.
  • D: The Anti-Federalists feared that a distant, powerful central government would resemble monarchy; they wanted power kept in the states. They did not favor monarchy itself.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u3-revolution-04

After the American victory at Saratoga in 1777, France signed treaties of alliance and commerce with the United States. Which broader context best explains France's decision?

  1. A France's dedication to spreading republican government, which the American cause embodied -- the alliance was an ideological crusade for liberty and shared revolutionary principles above all else.
  2. B Benjamin Franklin's personal popularity in Paris, which charmed the French court into gambling on the rebellion regardless of France's own interests.
  3. C France's certainty after Saratoga that American victory was now inevitable, which made the alliance a risk-free move to share in the spoils.
  4. D France's rivalry with Britain: humiliated by its Seven Years' War defeat, France seized the chance to weaken its old enemy once Saratoga proved the Americans could win.
Answer and explanation

Key: D

France was an absolute monarchy that feared republican ideas at home; it bankrolled the American revolution to avenge its 1763 defeat and cripple Britain, with American trade as a bonus. Saratoga mattered because it showed the rebellion could survive -- the war still had four years to run. (A) reads later ideals into a king's foreign policy. (B) shrinks a great-power decision to one man's charm. (C) confuses a promising sign with a certain outcome.

  • A: Wrong. This reads later ideals back into an absolute monarchy. France's government opposed republicanism at home; its motives were strategic -- weakening Britain -- not ideological.
  • B: Wrong. Franklin's diplomacy helped, but no one man's popularity explains a great-power alliance. France acted on its own strategic interests, not on charm.
  • C: Wrong. In early 1778 nothing was certain; Britain still held New York and would campaign for years. Saratoga persuaded France the Americans were a worthwhile bet, not a guaranteed winner.
  • D: Correct. Placing the alliance inside the long Bourbon-British rivalry explains what ideology cannot: why an absolute monarchy bankrolled a republican revolution -- to avenge its Seven Years' War defeat and break British power.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u3-seven-years-war-01
A 1763 memorandum from a British treasury official argues that because the war left Britain deeply in debt, the colonies — which had grown rich from wartime contracts and trade — should now help pay the empire's costs through new parliamentary taxes.

Which of the following best evaluates the reasoning of the memorandum's argument?

  1. A It is sound: Britain's war debt made new taxes necessary, and the colonies' wartime profits show they could afford to pay their fair share of the empire's costs.
  2. B It is sound because taxation always follows a major war, so the colonists' objections must really have been about the size of the tax bills rather than about Parliament's authority to impose them at all.
  3. C It is flawed: wartime profits went mostly to coastal merchants and contractors, while frontier regions endured raids and occupation — the premise of uniform colonial enrichment does not hold.
  4. D It is sound: colonial assemblies had already paid for the entire war effort out of their own treasuries, so the new taxes were clearly meant to punish colonial disloyalty rather than to raise needed revenue.
Answer and explanation

Key: C

The memorandum treats 'the colonies' as a single economy, but the war's costs and profits fell very unevenly. Port-city merchants and army contractors grew rich, while Pennsylvania's frontier absorbed devastating raids. The deeper flaw is not that taxes followed the war — they did — but that the argument builds its case on a false picture of shared colonial prosperity. Colonial objections, meanwhile, centered on Parliament's authority to tax at all, not on the size of the bill.

  • A: This accepts the memorandum's premise without examining it. Sound evaluation requires checking whether the evidence — here, the claim that the colonies as a whole grew rich — actually supports the conclusion.
  • B: This confuses sequence with explanation: the fact that taxes followed the war does not by itself prove why they were imposed. It also misstates colonial objections, which were about Parliament's right to tax, not the amounts.
  • C: Correct. The argument overgeneralizes from the experience of some merchants and contractors to all colonists, ignoring the very different wartime experience of frontier regions. A premise that is false for large parts of the colonies cannot carry the conclusion.
  • D: This gets the history backwards: Britain bore enormous war costs and even reimbursed some colonial expenses; the colonies did not self-fund the war. The revenue acts were fiscal measures to service debt, not punishments for disloyalty.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u3-taxation-02
A 1768 Boston newspaper essay urging merchants to keep up the nonimportation boycott of British goods declares: 'Parliament understands only the language of trade. Our last refusal bent them; this one will break them.'

Considering the author's purpose and historical situation, which statement best evaluates the essay's claim?

  1. A The claim is accurate: the colonial boycott alone forced Parliament to repeal the Stamp Act in 1766, with British merchants and the new Rockingham ministry playing no real part whatsoever in that decision or its timing.
  2. B The claim proves that the colonies had already become economically independent of Britain by 1768, needing neither British goods nor British markets to thrive.
  3. C The essay is written to persuade merchants to stay in the boycott, and it oversimplifies history: the 1766 repeal also reflected lobbying by British merchants hurt by the boycott and a change of ministry in London.
  4. D The claim is false because Parliament never repealed any colonial tax in response to colonial pressure, either in 1766 or at any later date.
Answer and explanation

Key: C

The essay is a pep talk, not a history lesson — its job is to keep merchants from breaking ranks, so it presents the boycott as an all-powerful weapon. Nonimportation did matter: it squeezed British exporters, who pressured Parliament. But the 1766 repeal also came from a new Rockingham ministry eager to undo Grenville's policies. Treating the boycott as the sole cause, or as proof of economic independence, reads a sales pitch as a complete explanation.

  • A: This takes the essay's boast at face value and assigns a single cause to a multi-causal event. The boycott contributed, but British merchant lobbying and the fall of Grenville's ministry were also decisive.
  • B: A boycott is a pressure tactic, not proof of independence — its very purpose was to inflict pain through the existing trade relationship. Reading the rhetoric literally mistakes a weapon for a description of the economy.
  • C: Correct. Recognizing the essay as persuasion aimed at a specific audience (merchants wavering on the boycott) reveals its limits as evidence: it simplifies a complex repeal into a single heroic cause to keep its readers committed.
  • D: This is factually wrong. Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766 and most of the Townshend duties in 1770, both under colonial pressure. The error is in the history, not just the reasoning.

MCQoriginal-hard-u4-missouri-compromise-02

A historian argues that the Missouri Compromise of 1820 resolved the sectional crisis over the expansion of slavery. Which additional evidence would most call that argument into question?

  1. A Missouri entered the Union as a slave state while Maine entered as a free state, keeping the Senate evenly balanced, which proves the crisis was settled
  2. B Congress repealed the Compromise's 36°30' restriction on slavery's expansion in the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854
  3. C The Compromise failed because it did not abolish slavery, and only abolition could have resolved the crisis
  4. D The nation avoided war over slavery until 1861, which shows the Compromise kept the crisis resolved for forty years
Answer and explanation

Key: B

The Compromise calmed the immediate crisis with Senate balance and the 36°30' line, but the settlement did not hold -- the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed that line, reopening the fight over slavery's expansion. A deal undone within a generation did not resolve the crisis, whatever the truce mechanism, Clay's reputation, or the quiet decades suggest.

  • A: Wrong. Senate balance was the mechanism of the truce, not proof that the underlying conflict was settled.
  • B: Right. Repealing the Compromise's core restriction shows the supposed 'resolution' failed within a generation.
  • C: Wrong. This judges an 1820 bargain by an abolition standard its makers never set; the question is whether the crisis was resolved, not whether slavery ended.
  • D: Wrong. Decades without war do not equal a resolved crisis -- the nullification fight and the gag-rule battles of the 1830s show the conflict kept burning.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u4-african-americans-02

A historian argues that in the 1820s and 1830s most free Black people in the North supported the American Colonization Society's plan to settle them in Liberia. Which evidence most undermines that argument?

  1. A The society's published appeals described colonization as a blessing for free Black people, so its stated good intentions prove that Black northerners supported the plan.
  2. B A few prominent Black leaders favored emigration to Africa, which shows that the colonization idea had genuine appeal among free Black people generally.
  3. C Liberia declared its independence in 1847, which proves that the society's plan eventually succeeded.
  4. D In 1817 thousands of free Black Philadelphians protested colonization, and Black newspapers in the 1820s denounced the society as a removal scheme.
Answer and explanation

Key: D

The claim is about what most free Black northerners believed, so the test is evidence from them. A mass protest of thousands in 1817 and sustained attacks on the society in Black newspapers directly contradict the idea of broad Black support. (A) confuses the society's sales pitch with its audience's opinion. (B) stretches a few leaders' views into a whole population's. (C) answers a different question -- what happened in Liberia in 1847 says nothing about Black opinion in the 1820s and 1830s.

  • A: Wrong. The society's published appeals show what it wanted people to believe, not what free Black northerners actually believed. Stated good intentions are not evidence of anyone else's opinion.
  • B: Wrong. A few Black leaders' interest in emigration cannot be stretched into the views of most free Black northerners, and independent emigrationism was not the same as supporting the ACS.
  • C: Wrong. What happened in Liberia in 1847 does not answer what free Black northerners believed in the 1820s and 1830s -- a later outcome is not evidence of earlier opinion.
  • D: Correct. It supplies direct evidence from free Black northerners themselves -- a mass protest and sustained Black newspaper opposition -- which directly undercuts the claim that most supported the society.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u4-america-on-the-world-stage-03
President James Monroe's 1823 message to Congress warned European powers against further colonization or intervention in the Americas (paraphrased).

A historian claims that the Monroe Doctrine made the United States the dominant power in the Western Hemisphere beginning in the 1820s. Which consideration most qualifies that claim?

  1. A The United States had only a small navy in the 1820s; it was Britain's Royal Navy, not American force, that truly discouraged European intervention.
  2. B Because no European power ever again established a colony in the Americas, the doctrine alone ended European imperialism in the entire Western Hemisphere.
  3. C Later presidents used the doctrine to justify sending troops abroad, which proves it gave the United States enforcement power from 1823.
  4. D Spain's empire was already collapsing, so by the 1820s no European power had any interest left in the Americas.
Answer and explanation

Key: A

The doctrine was a bold statement, but the United States had only a small navy and army in the 1820s and could not have stopped a determined European power on its own. Britain's Royal Navy — motivated by British trade interests in Latin America — was the real deterrent, which means the doctrine's force depended on a power the United States did not control. European interest in the hemisphere had not vanished either: Russia was pressing claims in the Pacific Northwest.

  • A: Right. It qualifies the claim by showing the United States lacked the force to back its words — British sea power, not American power, did the deterring in the 1820s.
  • B: Wrong. It treats the doctrine as the single cause of everything that followed and overstates the outcome — European powers did intervene in the hemisphere again, as France did in Mexico in the 1860s.
  • C: Wrong. It projects later presidents' uses of the doctrine backward onto 1823. How the doctrine was used decades later does not show what power the United States held when it was proclaimed.
  • D: Wrong. European powers still had real interests in the Americas — Russia's 1821 claims in the Pacific Northwest were one of the reasons Monroe issued the message at all.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u4-expanding-democracy-05

A historian writes: 'By the 1840s, Jacksonian democracy had made the United States a fully democratic nation.' Which evaluation of this claim is most accurate?

  1. A It is accurate: voter turnout reached record levels in 1840, which proves that all Americans could participate in politics.
  2. B It is accurate: Andrew Jackson personally ended property requirements for voting, making him the single cause of American democracy.
  3. C It overstates the case: property barriers for white men largely fell, but women, enslaved people, and most free Black men could not vote.
  4. D It is inaccurate: eastern states kept property requirements for voting until after the Civil War, while only western states democratized.
Answer and explanation

Key: C

The claim overstates the change. Property requirements for white men did fall away in most states by the 1840s, and turnout surged — but 'fully democratic' ignores that women, enslaved people, and most free Black men could not vote at all. The expansion was real but bounded: it democratized politics for white men, not for all Americans.

  • A: Wrong. High turnout shows that many of those allowed to vote did so; it does not show that everyone was allowed. Participation by the included says nothing about the excluded.
  • B: Wrong. It credits one man with the whole change. Property requirements were already falling before Jackson took office and kept falling after — legislatures, not Jackson alone, made those changes.
  • C: Right. It accepts the real expansion to white men while naming the groups still shut out, which is exactly where 'fully democratic' fails.
  • D: Wrong. It reverses the regional pattern: most eastern states had dropped property qualifications by the 1840s, and western states were not the lone holdouts of democracy.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u4-jackson-and-federal-power-01
President Andrew Jackson's 1832 veto of the bill rechartering the Bank of the United States: "It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes."

A historian wants to use this veto message to measure how the Bank of the United States actually affected ordinary borrowers. What most limits the message for that purpose?

  1. A The message was addressed only to members of Congress, so it reveals nothing about how ordinary Americans viewed the Bank.
  2. B Written as an election-year appeal against the Bank, it offers accusations but no loan or price figures, so it cannot by itself establish the Bank's economic effects.
  3. C Jackson's well-known hostility to all banks and paper money means every claim in the message is false, so historians should ignore this source entirely.
  4. D Congress overrode the veto within weeks of its delivery in July 1832, which shows that even the lawmakers who received it rejected the message's claims about the Bank.
Answer and explanation

Key: B

A veto message is political persuasion, not an economic study. Jackson issued it in 1832 while running for reelection, and Henry Clay's supporters had forced the recharter vote precisely to make the Bank a campaign issue. Because its purpose was to win votes, it asserts harm without offering any lending or price figures — so a historian needs other evidence to measure the Bank's real effects, and should not discard the source but recognize what it can and cannot show. Congress sustained the veto; no override ever occurred.

  • A: Wrong. The message was printed in newspapers and circulated nationwide as campaign material, so its audience included voters, not just Congress. The limit is its persuasive purpose, not its addressee.
  • B: Right. It identifies the source's election-year purpose and the specific gap — no economic data — that limits its use for measuring the Bank's actual effects on borrowers.
  • C: Wrong. A source's bias limits what it can prove; it does not make every claim false or the source useless. Historians use biased sources by asking what each source is fit to show.
  • D: Wrong. Congress sustained Jackson's veto; no override occurred. The recharter simply died, and Jackson won reelection in 1832.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u4-market-revolution-industrialization-04
An 1840s issue of the Lowell Offering, a magazine written by women working in Lowell's textile mills, describes the boardinghouses as comfortable and mill work as compatible with education and self-improvement (paraphrased).

A historian wants to use this magazine to describe daily working conditions in the Lowell mills. What most limits the magazine for that purpose?

  1. A Because the articles were written by mill workers themselves, the magazine gives only the workers' viewpoint and ignores the mill owners' perspective entirely.
  2. B The magazine was published in the 1840s, after the Lowell system had already declined, so it describes conditions that no longer existed.
  3. C The operatives who wrote for it were Irish immigrants, whose experiences differed from those of native-born workers.
  4. D The magazine appeared with the companies' approval to answer public criticism of factory life, so its cheerful picture served the companies' interests too.
Answer and explanation

Key: D

The Offering was written by operatives, but it appeared with the mill companies' approval and was created partly to answer public criticism of factory life. A publication designed to defend the mill system will naturally emphasize its pleasant side, so its cheerful picture cannot be taken as a neutral record of conditions. The early Lowell workforce was also native-born farm daughters from New England, not immigrants.

  • A: Wrong. The problem is not that it shows only one side's viewpoint — the problem is that the cheerful side shown served the companies' interest in defending the mill system, since the magazine needed their approval.
  • B: Wrong. The Lowell Offering ran from 1840 to 1845, squarely during the Lowell system's operation, so its timing is not the issue.
  • C: Wrong. The early Lowell operatives were native-born New England farm daughters; large-scale Irish immigration to the mills came later, in the late 1840s and 1850s.
  • D: Right. It identifies the editorial situation — company approval and a defensive purpose aimed at critics — that limits the magazine's use as a neutral record of working conditions.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u4-politics-and-regional-interests-08

One historian argues the nullification crisis was fundamentally about the tariff; another argues it was fundamentally about slavery. Which statement best evaluates these competing interpretations?

  1. A The tariff-only interpretation is correct, because South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification named the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 and said nothing about slavery, so slavery played no role in the crisis.
  2. B The slavery interpretation is correct, because South Carolina nullified the tariffs in order to shield the slave trade from heavy federal taxation.
  3. C Neither is correct: the crisis was really driven by the personal rivalry between Andrew Jackson and John C. Calhoun, which turned a routine policy dispute into a constitutional crisis.
  4. D Each captures part of the truth: the tariffs were the immediate grievance, but South Carolina's leaders feared that yielding tariff power would open the way to federal action against slavery.
Answer and explanation

Key: D

The immediate fight was over the tariffs of 1828 and 1832, which South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification explicitly named — so the tariff interpretation is not wrong about the trigger. But South Carolina's leaders, led by Calhoun, feared that conceding Congress's power to impose protective tariffs would concede its power over slavery itself. Treating it as either-or misses how the tariff fight was, for its leaders, also a rehearsal for defending slavery.

  • A: Wrong. What a document names is its stated grievance, not necessarily its deepest motive. Reading the ordinance literally rules out the slavery fear that Calhoun and others expressed privately.
  • B: Wrong. The tariffs taxed imported manufactured goods, not the slave trade. This invents a mechanism that did not exist to make the slavery interpretation work.
  • C: Wrong. It reduces a constitutional crisis to personalities. Jackson and Calhoun did clash, but personal rivalry does not explain the doctrine of nullification or the tariff grievances behind it.
  • D: Right. It holds both interpretations at once: the tariffs were the real and immediate grievance, and the deeper fear was that federal tariff power implied federal power over slavery.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u4-second-great-awakening-06
An 1826 revival sermon urges listeners to give up drinking and sign a temperance pledge (paraphrased).

A historian cites this sermon as evidence that the Second Great Awakening reduced drinking in American communities. Which additional evidence would best support that claim?

  1. A Church membership rolls showing how many new members joined congregations after revivals were held.
  2. B Temperance society pledge lists and estimates of per-capita alcohol consumption in towns where revivals took place.
  3. C The sermon's frequent reprinting, which shows that large numbers of Americans heard its message.
  4. D The minister's autobiography, in which he recalls that hundreds signed temperance pledges after hearing him preach.
Answer and explanation

Key: B

A sermon shows what the minister urged, not what listeners did — persuasion is not proof of changed behavior. The best test is behavioral evidence: pledge lists showing who actually signed, and consumption estimates showing whether drinking fell in revival towns. Membership rolls and reprint counts show reach, not results, and the minister's own memory is self-interested.

  • A: Wrong. Joining a church is not the same as giving up drink. Membership rolls measure revival reach, not whether drinking behavior changed.
  • B: Right. Pledge lists record actual commitments and consumption estimates measure actual drinking — the behavioral evidence the claim about reduced drinking requires.
  • C: Wrong. Wide reprinting shows the message traveled far; it does not show that anyone acted on it. The spread of an argument is not evidence the argument worked.
  • D: Wrong. The minister had every reason to remember his own preaching as successful. A self-interested recollection is weaker than independent records of what people did.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u4-south-society-07
In an 1837 Senate speech, a Southern leader called slavery a 'positive good' that protected both Black and white Southerners (paraphrased).

A historian cites this speech to argue that slavery in the South was a benevolent institution. Which consideration most weakens that use of the speech?

  1. A The speaker owned enslaved laborers himself, so only evidence drawn from his own plantation -- not abolitionist pamphlets -- could truly confirm or refute his description of slavery as a whole.
  2. B After 1837 Southern writers largely stopped criticizing slavery in print, which strongly suggests that conditions for enslaved people must have improved.
  3. C It was a political defense against abolitionist attacks, and the forced movement of about a million enslaved people through the domestic slave trade contradicts its benevolent picture.
  4. D Because Northern factory workers also faced harsh and dangerous conditions, slavery was really no worse than the wage labor system of the North.
Answer and explanation

Key: C

Calhoun delivered the 'positive good' speech as a political counterattack on abolitionists, not as a neutral description — it was designed to defend, so it cannot be read as a plain report of conditions. And the record contradicts the benevolent picture: the domestic slave trade forcibly moved roughly a million enslaved people, separating families, while enslaved people resisted in ways from sabotage to rebellion. Comparing slavery to Northern factory labor was itself part of the pro-slavery argument, not independent evidence.

  • A: Wrong. His ownership does not make his plantation a valid stand-in for the whole South, and it misses the real problem: the speech was political defense, not a field report, wherever it was written.
  • B: Wrong. Southerners stopped criticizing slavery because abolitionist attacks made open criticism politically dangerous, not because conditions improved. A change in rhetoric is not a change in conditions.
  • C: Right. It identifies the speech's defensive purpose — aimed at abolitionists — and brings outside evidence (forced family separation, resistance) that contradicts the benevolent portrait.
  • D: Wrong. The 'wage slavery' comparison was itself a pro-slavery talking point. Accepting the comparison at face value repeats the argument instead of testing it.

MCQoriginal-hard-u5-compromise-1850-06

A textbook states that the Compromise of 1850 settled the sectional crisis over slavery in the territories. Which evidence gives the strongest reason to doubt that conclusion?

  1. A Because the compromise passed in 1850 and war did not come until 1861, the compromise must have kept the peace for eleven years, which is the only explanation needed for why the nation avoided war during that decade.
  2. B Northern outrage over the Fugitive Slave Act -- including personal liberty laws and mass protest -- deepened sectional hostility instead of calming it.
  3. C California's admission as a free state permanently satisfied Southern demands about the territories.
  4. D Both sections voted for the compromise measures, which proves slavery was no longer a divisive issue after 1850.
Answer and explanation

Key: B

The compromise's Fugitive Slave Act forced Northerners to participate in returning escapees, sparking personal liberty laws, rescues, and Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin. A bargain that inflames one side's resistance has not settled the crisis, whatever the vote counts suggest.

  • A: Wrong. That eleven years passed between the compromise and the war does not show the compromise caused the peace; the 1850s were filled with escalating crises. This confuses sequence with causation.
  • B: Correct. The backlash to the Fugitive Slave Act is direct evidence that the compromise deepened rather than resolved sectional hostility.
  • C: Wrong. California's admission as a free state alarmed the South by tipping the Senate balance against slavery's expansion, the opposite of satisfying Southern demands.
  • D: Wrong. Passing a package of bills is not the same as resolving the underlying conflict; congressional votes cannot settle what the public keeps fighting over.

MCQoriginal-hard-u5-dred-scott-10

A student argues: "The Dred Scott decision settled the question of slavery in the territories, so the Lincoln-Douglas debates of 1858 were pointless." Which response best evaluates that argument?

  1. A The student is right: a Supreme Court ruling is the final word in American law, so the territorial question was closed and the 1858 debates must have been about other issues
  2. B The decision inflamed the conflict instead of settling it -- it outraged Republicans and forced Douglas to invent the Freeport Doctrine.
  3. C The debates happened after the ruling, so they could not have influenced the ruling -- which means they served no purpose
  4. D The case concerned one man's freedom suit, so its ruling could not have affected slavery anywhere beyond Dred Scott himself
Answer and explanation

Key: B

Taney's ruling tried to remove slavery from politics by judicial fiat and achieved the opposite: Republicans treated it as proof of a proslavery conspiracy, and Douglas's Freeport answer -- that territories could exclude slavery by refusing to pass slave codes -- split the Democrats. A decision nobody accepts has settled nothing, and the debates' timing or the case's parties do not change that.

  • A: Wrong. A Supreme Court ruling settles the law, not the politics -- the fierce public reaction to Dred Scott is proof that a pronouncement settles nothing when the public rejects it.
  • B: Right. The decision outraged the North and forced new political maneuvering, inflaming rather than settling the territorial question.
  • C: Wrong. That the debates could not change the ruling does not make them pointless -- they were aimed at voters in an election, not at the Court.
  • D: Wrong. The ruling went far beyond Scott himself, declaring Congress powerless to ban slavery in the territories.

MCQoriginal-hard-u5-emancipation-proclamation-05

The Emancipation Proclamation (January 1, 1863) declared free the enslaved people in areas still in rebellion. What best explains the timing of Lincoln's decision to issue it?

  1. A After the Union victory at Antietam, Lincoln could present emancipation as a war measure -- one that discouraged Britain and France from aiding the Confederacy and opened the door to Black military service.
  2. B Northern public opinion in 1862 demanded immediate universal abolition, and elected leaders in a democracy simply carry out what the majority wants, so Lincoln was merely obeying the voters rather than making any strategic choice of his own.
  3. C The proclamation freed every enslaved person in the United States, finishing the work of abolition in a single stroke.
  4. D Abolitionist persuasion finally convinced Lincoln that slavery was morally wrong, which is the only reason he waited until 1863.
Answer and explanation

Key: A

Antietam gave Lincoln the military credibility to act; framing emancipation as a war measure let him strike at the Confederacy's labor force, make the war about slavery in European eyes, and authorize Black enlistment. The proclamation did not free everyone -- it exempted loyal border states -- and Northern opinion was far from unified, so neither a democratic mandate nor moral conversion alone explains the timing.

  • A: Correct. The timing follows a Union victory, and the measure's military and diplomatic functions -- deterring Europe, adding Black soldiers -- explain why late 1862 was the moment.
  • B: Wrong. This projects a modern assumption about leaders following majority opinion onto 1862, when Northern opinion on abolition was deeply divided.
  • C: Wrong. The proclamation exempted the loyal border states and areas already under Union control; full abolition required the Thirteenth Amendment.
  • D: Wrong. This reduces a strategic military and diplomatic decision to a single moral cause, ignoring why Lincoln acted when he did.

MCQoriginal-hard-u5-free-soil-wilmot-03

A historian claims that Northern opposition to the Mexican-American War was driven less by pacifism than by fear that conquered territory would become new slave states. Which additional evidence would best support that claim?

  1. A Several Northern congressmen gave speeches calling the war immoral, which proves Northern opposition was driven by pacifist principle rather than politics
  2. B The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo gave the United States a vast Mexican Cession, which proves that most Northerners supported the war once they saw what it gained
  3. C The Wilmot Proviso of 1846, which attempted to ban slavery in any territory acquired from Mexico
  4. D Henry David Thoreau spent a night in jail rather than pay the tax that funded the war, which shows Northern opposition was a mass pacifist movement
Answer and explanation

Key: C

The Wilmot Proviso directly ties Northern antiwar politics to antislavery: its supporters opposed taking Mexican land precisely because they feared slavery would follow the flag. Moral language in antiwar speeches does not show the speakers opposed war on principle, the treaty's gains cannot reveal anyone's motives, and Thoreau's protest was one man's stand rather than a mass movement.

  • A: Wrong. Taking the moral language of antiwar speeches at face value proves nothing about pacifism -- for many Northern critics, the war was 'immoral' precisely because it threatened to extend slavery, which is the historian's point rather than an alternative to it.
  • B: Wrong. The treaty records what the war gained; the gains cannot show whether most Northerners supported the war, and what people thought after the fact says nothing about why opponents opposed it.
  • C: Right. The proviso is direct evidence that Northern opponents of the war acted to block slavery's expansion into conquered territory.
  • D: Wrong. Thoreau's individual protest cannot stand in for a mass movement; one famous jail night does not show what Northern opposition generally looked like.

MCQoriginal-hard-u5-reconstruction-turning-point-08

One historian argues that Reconstruction fundamentally changed the lives of African Americans; another argues it changed almost nothing. Which pairing of evidence best explains why historians disagree about this period?

  1. A Most freedpeople remained landless laborers after the war, and segregation became law across the South by the 1890s, which proves federal policy made no real difference
  2. B The Reconstruction amendments stayed on paper only, since segregation returned, so the legal changes of the 1860s had no real significance
  3. C Because federal troops left the South in 1877, everything accomplished before that date was canceled and no longer counts as change
  4. D The amendments and Black voting and officeholding broke legally with slavery, while sharecropping and racial terror preserved much of the old order.
Answer and explanation

Key: D

Both sides of the disagreement have real evidence: emancipation, citizenship, voting rights, and Black legislators were genuine breaks with the past, yet most freedpeople remained trapped in debt, dependent labor, and violence. Explaining the disagreement means holding both halves of the record at once -- neither the changes nor the continuities can be argued away.

  • A: Wrong. Economic hardship after the war was real, but it does not erase the constitutional changes -- hardship in daily life and legal transformation can both be true.
  • B: Wrong. That the amendments were unevenly enforced does not make their text meaningless; the gap between law and practice is not proof the law changed nothing.
  • C: Wrong. That federal troops left in 1877 does not retroactively cancel what happened before 1877; an endpoint cannot erase real changes.
  • D: Right. Genuine legal and political breaks coexisted with deep economic and social continuities, which is exactly why historians keep disagreeing.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u5-civil-war-military-05
A historian writes: 'The Battle of Gettysburg, July 1-3, 1863, was the decisive turning point of the Civil War.'

Which consideration best qualifies the historian's claim?

  1. A Gettysburg produced the war's highest casualty count, which confirms that it was the most important battle.
  2. B Gettysburg fell almost exactly at the midpoint of the war, so the calendar alone marks it as the turn from Confederate to Union advantage -- the first half belonged to the South, the second half to the North.
  3. C Vicksburg surrendered to Grant on July 4, 1863, giving the Union the Mississippi and splitting the Confederacy -- so singling out Gettysburg ignores a simultaneous victory of comparable strategic weight.
  4. D Lee's defeat at Gettysburg destroyed the Army of Northern Virginia, leaving the Confederacy with no effective field army.
Answer and explanation

Key: C

A turning-point claim has to survive comparison with rival candidates. Vicksburg fell the day after Gettysburg ended and achieved a long-standing Union strategic goal -- opening the Mississippi -- while the war then continued for nearly two more years. Gettysburg mattered, but calling it the decisive turn requires ignoring what happened simultaneously in the West.

  • A: Wrong. Casualty totals measure cost, not strategic effect; the bloodiest battle isn't automatically the most decisive one.
  • B: Wrong. Falling near the middle of the timeline doesn't make a battle the cause of what followed -- that's the calendar doing the arguing.
  • C: Right. It introduces competing evidence -- a simultaneous Union victory of major strategic consequence -- that forces the turning-point claim to be qualified.
  • D: Wrong. Lee's army retreated intact and kept fighting for almost two more years; Gettysburg weakened it but did not destroy it.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u5-emancipation-06
The Emancipation Proclamation (January 1, 1863) declared free the enslaved people in states and parts of states then in rebellion. It exempted the loyal slave states -- Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, and Missouri -- and areas already under Union control.

Given these exemptions, which conclusion about Lincoln's purposes is best supported?

  1. A Lincoln framed emancipation as a war measure, aiming to weaken the Confederacy's labor force and add Black soldiers to Union ranks while keeping the loyal slave states in the Union.
  2. B The exemptions prove Lincoln did not truly oppose slavery and issued the Proclamation only as a hollow gesture, since a president who meant it would never have left anyone in bondage anywhere in the country.
  3. C The exemptions were meaningless because the Proclamation freed every enslaved person in the United States on the day it was issued.
  4. D Lincoln should have freed everyone at once regardless of military consequences, which shows the Proclamation was a moral failure.
Answer and explanation

Key: A

The pattern of the exemptions is the clue: Lincoln acted under his war powers as commander in chief, so the Proclamation reached only where he claimed military authority -- the rebelling areas. That same war-powers logic explains the strategy: deprive the Confederacy of labor, gain soldiers (about 180,000 Black men served in the Union army), and hold the border states. The exemptions reveal purpose, not insincerity.

  • A: Right. It connects the exemption pattern to the war-powers justification and then to the concrete military aims -- each step follows from the last.
  • B: Wrong. A limited, strategic use of emancipation isn't proof of indifference -- Lincoln had long opposed slavery's expansion, and the Proclamation's design follows from its legal basis as a war measure.
  • C: Wrong. The Proclamation freed no one in the loyal border states or in Union-held areas on the day it was issued; its reach was deliberately limited.
  • D: Wrong. Judging Lincoln's wartime choices by what a modern observer would demand ignores the legal and political constraints he was actually navigating.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u5-failure-of-compromise-03
The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) repealed the Missouri Compromise line and left the slavery question in the Kansas and Nebraska territories to the settlers themselves -- 'popular sovereignty.'

A student argues that popular sovereignty was a workable democratic solution and failed only because it was never honestly tried. Which fact best qualifies that claim?

  1. A The Kansas-Nebraska Act was written by Stephen Douglas mainly to win Southern support for a transcontinental railroad through Chicago, which means the slavery controversy was only a side issue he never intended to provoke.
  2. B Southerners rejected popular sovereignty because they opposed democratic self-government on principle.
  3. C It was tried: pro-slavery Missourians crossed into Kansas to vote fraudulently, and settlers formed rival pro-slavery and free-state governments, so the procedure produced rival authorities instead of a decision.
  4. D Because Kansas entered the Union as a free state in 1861, popular sovereignty eventually produced the result its supporters intended.
Answer and explanation

Key: C

The claim assumes the mechanism never got a fair test. But Kansas did hold territorial elections -- and they were corrupted by cross-border voting fraud while each side set up its own government (pro-slavery at Lecompton, free-state at Topeka). The breakdown was in the procedure itself, not just in people's willingness to try it.

  • A: Wrong. Douglas did want a railroad, but reducing the whole Act to one man's railroad scheme ignores the slavery-extension fight that made it explosive.
  • B: Wrong. Southern opposition was about protecting slavery's expansion, not a rejection of democracy -- many Southerners demanded a federal slave code instead.
  • C: Right. It brings direct evidence -- fraudulent elections and rival governments -- that the mechanism was tested and failed on its own terms.
  • D: Wrong. Kansas's 1861 admission came after Southern senators had left Congress; the free-state outcome reflected secession, not the success of popular sovereignty.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u5-failure-of-reconstruction-08
Under the Compromise of 1877, Rutherford B. Hayes became president and the last federal troops were withdrawn from South Carolina, Florida, and Louisiana.

Which evidence best qualifies the claim that the Compromise of 1877 caused the end of Reconstruction?

  1. A The Panic of 1873 alone ended Reconstruction by destroying Northern interest in Southern affairs and making further federal intervention politically impossible for the rest of the decade.
  2. B The Compromise restored slavery-era Black Codes across the South.
  3. C After 1877 the federal government took no further action on civil rights until the 1960s.
  4. D By 1876 white Democrats had already retaken control of every other Southern state, so the Compromise removed the last troops rather than single-handedly reversing Reconstruction.
Answer and explanation

Key: D

The Compromise matters, but it was the last step, not the whole story. 'Redemption' -- white Democrats regaining state governments, often through violence and fraud -- had already succeeded nearly everywhere by 1876; only three states still had Republican governments with federal troops. The Compromise finished a process that was mostly complete, so treating it as the sole cause overstates its role.

  • A: Wrong. The depression of 1873 did shift Northern attention, but one economic shock can't carry the whole explanation -- violence, court rulings, and political deals all played parts.
  • B: Wrong. The Black Codes dated to 1865-66 and were answered by the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the Fourteenth Amendment -- a decade before the Compromise.
  • C: Wrong. Federal civil-rights action didn't vanish for eighty years -- Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1875, for example, even though the Supreme Court struck it down in 1883.
  • D: Right. It puts the Compromise in sequence: the troops it withdrew were the last of a dwindling presence, so 1877 capped a longer unraveling rather than causing it alone.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u5-manifest-destiny-01
Adapted from an 1845 editorial by Democratic journalist John L. O'Sullivan urging the annexation of Texas: the United States has a God-given mission to spread across the whole continent, extending liberty and self-government to new lands.

For a historian investigating why the United States annexed Texas in 1845, what is the most important limitation of this passage as evidence?

  1. A It proves that Congress annexed Texas because a majority of Americans believed Providence commanded the United States to expand.
  2. B It shows what expansionists hoped annexation would mean, but as advocacy written to persuade, it reveals its supporters' aims more than the contested debate over slavery and war behind the decision.
  3. C It cannot be used at all, because its assumptions about American superiority would be condemned by modern standards.
  4. D It demonstrates that the idea of expansion was invented in 1845, so the earlier American settlement of Texas under Mexican land grants in the 1820s had no connection to the annexation debate at all.
Answer and explanation

Key: B

O'Sullivan wrote to persuade, not to record. The passage is strong evidence of how Democratic expansionists framed annexation, but a historian also needs the opposition -- Whig warnings about war with Mexico and the fight over slavery's expansion -- to explain why annexation happened when and how it did. Taking one editorial as the whole story would mistake advocacy for the full decision-making process.

  • A: Wrong. This treats one editor's rallying cry as proof of what moved Congress -- confusing persuasive rhetoric with the actual reasons policymakers acted.
  • B: Right. The passage's purpose -- to win readers to annexation -- is exactly what limits it: it shows the expansionist case, not the contested political fight over slavery, war, and sectional balance that decided the issue.
  • C: Wrong. Historians can learn from sources whose values differ from ours; judging the passage by today's standards doesn't tell us what it can or cannot prove about 1845.
  • D: Wrong. Americans had been settling Texas since the 1820s; O'Sullivan coined a phrase in 1845, but the idea and the migration long predated him.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u5-mexican-war-02
President James K. Polk's war message to Congress, May 11, 1846: 'Mexico has passed the boundary of the United States, has invaded our territory and shed American blood upon the American soil.'

Which additional fact would most weaken Polk's claim in this passage?

  1. A Polk was a Democrat, and Democratic presidents of this era consistently sought territorial expansion.
  2. B Congress declared war two days later, which confirms that Mexico had indeed invaded American territory.
  3. C Texas had become a state the previous December, so an attack anywhere on Texan soil was legally an attack on the United States, regardless of where Mexico drew the boundary.
  4. D The April 1846 clash occurred in the strip between the Nueces River and the Rio Grande, land Texas claimed but Mexico had never accepted as Texan.
Answer and explanation

Key: D

Polk's case rested on the idea that the blood was shed on unquestionably American soil. But the boundary of Texas itself was disputed: Texas claimed the Rio Grande, Mexico claimed the Nueces, and Taylor's army was operating in the contested zone. That dispute doesn't settle who was morally right, but it directly undercuts the claim that Mexico invaded clearly American territory.

  • A: Wrong. Polk's party doesn't prove anything about the boundary facts; a party label can't substitute for evidence about where the fighting happened.
  • B: Wrong. Congress voting for war shows it accepted Polk's framing, not that his description of the boundary was accurate.
  • C: Wrong. Statehood didn't resolve where Texas ended -- Mexico still claimed the Nueces line, so 'Texan soil' was exactly what was in dispute.
  • D: Right. If the fighting happened in territory whose ownership was itself contested, Polk's claim of an invasion of American soil loses its foundation.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u5-reconstruction-07
A historian argues: 'Reconstruction was a political failure, but it produced lasting constitutional change.'

Which later development best supports the historian's claim?

  1. A The Fifteenth Amendment ended racial discrimination in voting when it was ratified in 1870, guaranteeing Black men an effective ballot throughout the South for generations to come.
  2. B The Fourteenth Amendment's guarantees of due process and equal protection became the legal foundation for twentieth-century court decisions striking down segregation.
  3. C The Fourteenth Amendment ended segregation as soon as it was ratified in 1868, since a constitutional amendment changes society the moment it becomes law.
  4. D When federal Reconstruction ended in 1877, the Reconstruction amendments were repealed along with it, so none of their guarantees carried into the twentieth century.
Answer and explanation

Key: B

The claim has two halves -- political failure, constitutional endurance -- and only one option connects a Reconstruction measure to a later result. The Fourteenth Amendment outlived the Reconstruction governments and gave twentieth-century courts the equal-protection language they used against segregation. (A) overstates the Fifteenth Amendment, which Southern states evaded with literacy tests, poll taxes, and white primaries. (C) confuses a law's ratification with instant social change -- amendments take effect as law, but segregation persisted for generations. (D) gets a basic fact wrong: the amendments stayed in the Constitution after 1877; what ended was federal enforcement.

  • A: Wrong. The Fifteenth Amendment barred denial of the vote by race, but Southern states soon used literacy tests, poll taxes, and white primaries to evade it.
  • B: Correct. It links the Reconstruction-era amendment to a concrete later result, showing constitutional change that endured after the politics collapsed.
  • C: Wrong. Ratification makes an amendment law, but it does not instantly remake society -- segregation persisted for generations after 1868.
  • D: Wrong. The amendments were never repealed; they stayed in the Constitution after 1877. What ended was federal enforcement in the South, not the amendments' legal force.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u5-secession-04
South Carolina's Declaration of the Immediate Causes of Secession, December 24, 1860: 'A geographical line has been drawn across the Union, and all the States north of that line have united in the election of a man to the high office of President of the United States, whose opinions and purposes are hostile to slavery.'

A historian using this document to explain South Carolina's secession should be most cautious about which of the following?

  1. A Treating the document as a complete account of motives: it was written to justify secession to other Southerners and the world, so it emphasizes the grievances most useful for legitimizing the decision.
  2. B Concluding that slavery drove secession, since the document frames its case around constitutional rights rather than the institution itself.
  3. C Using the document as evidence at all, since its authors were defending slavery and their arguments deserve no place in a historical explanation -- historians should rely instead on sources free of such moral taint.
  4. D Assuming other seceding states shared South Carolina's exact reasoning, since all Southern states faced the same election result.
Answer and explanation

Key: A

The declaration is an advocacy document, drafted to persuade -- first other Southern states, then the wider world -- that secession was justified. It is excellent evidence of the public case South Carolina's leaders chose to make, with slavery at its center, but its purpose shapes which grievances appear and how they are framed, so it cannot stand alone as the whole explanation.

  • A: Right. The document's purpose -- justifying a revolutionary act to sympathetic and skeptical audiences -- limits its use: it shows the chosen public case, not the unfiltered deliberations behind it.
  • B: Wrong. The passage states plainly that Lincoln's 'opinions and purposes are hostile to slavery' -- slavery is not hidden behind constitutional language here.
  • C: Wrong. A source doesn't become unusable because its authors defended something we condemn; historians explain the past, and this document is central evidence for why secessionists acted.
  • D: Wrong. One state's declaration can't speak for all eleven seceding states -- each held its own convention and made its own case.

MCQoriginal-hard-u6-gilded-age-politics-06

During the Gilded Age, presidential elections were fiercely contested, voter turnout often exceeded 75 percent, and the two parties were nearly evenly matched -- yet the federal government enacted few major domestic reforms. Which of the following best explains this apparent contradiction?

  1. A Voters turned out in large numbers because they expected the federal government to solve economic problems directly, as modern voters do
  2. B Because elections were so close, the parties must have differed sharply on major issues, which is what drove voters to the polls
  3. C Voters chose parties based on the tariff alone, so tariff policy explains both the high turnout and the lack of other reforms
  4. D Both parties were divided internally over tariffs, currency, and patronage, so neither could unite behind national reforms.
Answer and explanation

Key: D

Gilded Age parties were intensely competitive but internally fractured: Republicans and Democrats each contained pro- and anti-tariff wings, and the gold-versus-silver currency fight cut across both parties. That made it nearly impossible to assemble a majority for big national reforms, while voters still turned out in droves out of party loyalty, Civil War-era allegiances, and patronage ties. High participation and legislative stalemate were two sides of the same party system.

  • A: Wrong. This projects modern expectations onto the past. Gilded Age voters mobilized around party identity, Civil War loyalties, and patronage -- not around a belief that Washington should manage the economy.
  • B: Wrong. Close elections reflected two evenly matched party machines, not voters dividing sharply over issues; competitiveness alone does not show issue-driven voting.
  • C: Wrong. The tariff mattered, but one issue cannot explain both mass turnout and legislative stalemate -- the parties were internally divided on the tariff itself.
  • D: Right. Cross-cutting internal divisions over tariffs, currency, and patronage kept either party from uniting behind a national reform program, even as party loyalty and identity drove record turnout.

MCQoriginal-hard-u6-industrial-capitalism-04

Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890 to restrain monopolistic business combinations. Which of the following best evaluates the claim that the Act achieved its intended purpose during the 1890s?

  1. A The claim is supported because the Act's passage shows Congress was now regulating business aggressively, which means the era of noninterference had ended
  2. B The claim is weakened because the Act's earliest major courtroom uses targeted labor unions, as in the 1894 injunction against the Pullman strike.
  3. C The claim is weakened because the great merger wave of 1895-1904 came after the Act, which shows the law caused even more consolidation
  4. D The claim is supported because modern antitrust law descends from the Sherman Act, which proves it worked as intended from the start
Answer and explanation

Key: B

The Sherman Act was written to curb trusts, but in the 1890s prosecutors and courts turned it against unions -- most famously in the 1894 Pullman strike, when a federal court used the Act to enjoin Eugene Debs and the American Railway Union. The first major successful use against an actual corporate combination did not come until the Northern Securities case in 1904. Passing the law, the mergers that followed it, and its later reputation do not show it achieved its purpose in the 1890s.

  • A: Wrong. This confuses passing a law with achieving its goal. Congress can pass an antitrust law while enforcement goes in a different direction -- the statute's text is not evidence of its effects.
  • B: Right. The Act's earliest high-profile courtroom uses, including the 1894 Pullman strike injunction upheld in In re Debs (1895), were aimed at organized labor rather than at the corporate combinations the law was written to restrain.
  • C: Wrong. That the merger wave followed the Act does not prove the Act caused it; sequence is not causation, and consolidation grew for other reasons.
  • D: Wrong. That modern antitrust law descends from the Sherman Act shows its later significance, not that it achieved its intended purpose in the 1890s.

MCQoriginal-hard-u6-labor-gilded-age-01
In his 1889 essay 'The Gospel of Wealth,' steel magnate Andrew Carnegie argued that great fortunes were a natural and necessary product of civilization's progress, and that the wealthy should treat themselves as trustees bound to spend their surplus for the community's welfare.

Which of the following best evaluates the limits of using this essay as evidence about the experiences of steelworkers in the 1880s?

  1. A Because Carnegie openly acknowledged that inequality was inevitable, the essay shows that most workers accepted dangerous conditions as the price of progress
  2. B Because Carnegie was one of the richest and most successful industrialists, his account of industrial life is the most reliable one available
  3. C Carnegie's position as a steel magnate means the essay defends industrial fortunes, so it cannot substitute for evidence about workers' mill life.
  4. D Carnegie's call for the wealthy to give back shows he shared modern ideas of corporate responsibility, so the essay proves industrialists cared about workers
Answer and explanation

Key: C

Carnegie was one of the richest steelmakers in the world, and his essay is a defense of why men like him should keep their fortunes -- he had a direct interest in making great wealth look natural and good. That point of view shapes everything he says, so the essay tells us how industrialists justified their wealth, not what mill life was actually like for workers. A writer's claim about workers is not evidence of workers' views, his wealth does not make him reliable on their experience, and his call for giving does not show he shared modern values.

  • A: Wrong. This takes Carnegie's own claim -- that inequality was 'inevitable' -- as proof of what workers thought. A writer's assertion about workers is not evidence of workers' views, especially when the writer benefits from that assertion.
  • B: Wrong. Wealth and success do not make a source reliable about workers' experiences; Carnegie's position as an owner is exactly what limits the essay's use as evidence about mill life.
  • C: Right. A steel magnate defending industrial fortunes writes from the owner's side; his purpose is to justify wealth, which limits what the essay can show about workers' daily experiences.
  • D: Wrong. This projects modern ideas of corporate responsibility onto 1889; Carnegie's call for philanthropy served his defense of great fortunes, not a modern concern for workers.

MCQoriginal-hard-u6-westward-expansion-05

The Dawes Act of 1887 divided communally held tribal lands into individual allotments for Native American families, with the remaining 'surplus' land sold to non-Native settlers. Which of the following developments best explains why the Dawes Act took the form it did?

  1. A It continued the established federal practice of acquiring Native land through treaties negotiated with tribal leaders
  2. B Many Native families were already farming individually by the 1880s, so allotment merely recognized a change Native Americans had already made for themselves
  3. C It extended the post-Civil War federal campaign to open the West to railroads, mining, and settlers by breaking up tribal landholding
  4. D It was mainly an effort to help Native families build wealth like white homesteaders, as the law's supporters said when they promised allotment would 'civilize' Native Americans
Answer and explanation

Key: C

The Dawes Act fits a continuous federal push after the Civil War to transfer western land from Native nations to railroads, miners, and settlers -- the same campaign behind the transcontinental railroad land grants and the reservation wars of the 1870s. Allotment broke up tribal landholding so 'surplus' acres could be sold to non-Natives. It was not a treaty negotiation, it did not recognize changes Native families had made, and it is not explained by the reformers' own stated rationale.

  • A: Wrong. The Dawes Act imposed allotment unilaterally; Congress had ended treaty-making with tribes in 1871. This option projects an earlier pattern onto a later policy that broke with it.
  • B: Wrong. Some Native families farmed individually, but allotment was imposed on all tribal nations whether they farmed or not -- and the law's point was to declare most of the land 'surplus' and sell it. A change some families made cannot explain a policy forced on everyone.
  • C: Right. After the Civil War the federal government systematically worked to open the West to railroads, mining, and white settlement; the Dawes Act served that campaign by dissolving communal Native landholding and selling off the 'surplus.'
  • D: Wrong. The reformers' stated hope of 'civilizing' Native Americans through property was their justification for the policy, not the engine behind it -- the engine was transferring land to non-Native hands.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u6-labor-gilded-age-01
The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer with us to-day measures the change which has come with civilization. This change, however, is not to be deplored, but welcomed as highly beneficial. -- Andrew Carnegie, "Wealth," North American Review, 1889 (public domain)

Which of the following best evaluates how a historian studying labor relations in the 1890s could use this passage?

  1. A The passage is reliable evidence that factory workers' wages rose steadily, since Carnegie accurately measured the change industrial civilization had brought to workers' daily lives.
  2. B The passage is best used as evidence of how leading industrialists justified inequality; because Carnegie was one of the nation's largest employers, his claims about laborers' experience need corroboration from worker sources.
  3. C The passage proves that factory workers benefited from industrialization, which means the era's labor unrest was largely unnecessary and the American Federation of Labor's organizing drives addressed no genuine grievance at all.
  4. D Because Carnegie personally profited from the system he defends, nothing in the passage can be trusted, so historians of the 1890s should simply not use it at all.
Answer and explanation

Key: B

Carnegie writes as an employer defending the system that made him rich, so historians use this passage to study how industrialists justified inequality, not to learn what factory workers actually earned or felt. A self-serving source can still be valuable; what matters is matching the source to the question it can actually answer and checking its claims against other evidence.

  • A: Wrong. It takes Carnegie's argument as neutral fact. A justification written by one of the era's largest employers is not wage data, and accepting its claims about workers' lives repeats the source's own self-defense as if it were measurement.
  • B: Right. It names both the correct use (evidence of how industrialists justified inequality) and the limit (Carnegie's position as a major employer means his claims about workers need worker-source corroboration).
  • C: Wrong. It treats one man's defense of the system as proof of how workers actually fared, then uses that overgeneralization to erase the very grievances that produced the era's strikes and organizing.
  • D: Wrong. It makes the opposite error: declaring a biased source useless. Historians do not throw out self-interested sources; they analyze them for what they reveal about the author's purpose and position.

MCQoriginal-hard2-u6-role-of-government-01

A student claims that the federal government's commitment to laissez-faire economics during the Gilded Age meant it took no actions that benefited businesses. Which of the following best evaluates this claim?

  1. A The claim is valid: the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 shows the federal government took on big business rather than aiding it, confirming that Washington stayed neutral or hostile toward corporate growth.
  2. B The claim is valid: the Constitution barred the federal government from spending public money to aid private enterprise at any point before the Progressive Era, so whatever help firms received in these years had to come entirely from state and local governments.
  3. C The claim is invalid: the government granted millions of acres to railroads, kept high protective tariffs shielding manufacturers, and used federal troops and court injunctions to break strikes such as the Pullman strike of 1894.
  4. D The claim is invalid: laissez-faire economics directly caused the Great Depression, which proves that federal policy consistently damaged rather than helped American businesses.
Answer and explanation

Key: C

Laissez-faire in the Gilded Age meant the government refused to regulate business, not that it stood aside. Federal land grants to railroads, high protective tariffs for manufacturers, and troops and injunctions against strikers all actively helped business. The claim is wrong, and neither the Sherman Act on paper nor the Constitution kept Washington from acting on business's behalf.

  • A: Wrong. It confuses a law on the books with enforcement: the Sherman Act was barely used against trusts in its first decade and was instead used against labor, as in the 1894 Pullman strike. Passing a statute did not make the government neutral.
  • B: Wrong. Nothing in the Constitution prohibited federal aid to business, and no such aid ban existed; the railroad land grants and tariff protection of the period were federal actions.
  • C: Right. It refutes the claim with three concrete federal actions -- railroad land grants, protective tariffs, and the use of troops and injunctions against strikers -- each of which benefited business interests.
  • D: Wrong. The Great Depression began in 1929, decades after the Gilded Age ended, so it cannot directly prove anything about 1880s policy. It also gets the direction of federal help backwards.
