                                                  Evaluate the extent to which American participation in World War I fostered political, economic, and social change in the United States in the period from 1915 to 1935.

                                                    Documents
                                                    1. Document 1: Amendment to Section 3 of the Espionage Act (excerpt), June 15, 1917.

                                                      Whoever, when the United States is at war, shall willfully make or convey false reports or false statements with intent to interfere with the operation or success of the military or naval forces of the United States . . . or shall willfully obstruct . . . the recruiting or enlistment service of the United States, or . . . shall willfully utter, print, write, or publish any disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive language about the form of government of the United States, or the Constitution of the United States, or the military or naval forces of the United States . . . shall be punished.

                                                    2. Document 2: William Charles Morris, 'Mr. President, Why Not Make America Safe for Democracy?' The Kansas City Sun, July 14, 1917.

                                                      [Descriptive entry — no excerpted text in the source: an open letter from Black editor William Charles Morris arguing that President Wilson's crusade to 'make the world safe for democracy' required making America safe for democracy for Black Americans.]

                                                    3. Document 3: 'Another Tar and Feather Party Is Staged,' Ashland (Wisconsin) Daily Press, April 11, 1918.

                                                      Adolph Anton, residing at 1100 Sixth Avenue West, was taken from his home at about nine o'clock last night by a party of five or six who came to the house in an auto, carried to a spot on the Beaser Avenue road known as the Chequamego Ice Company's farm, and given a coat of tar and feathers for alleged pro-German sentiments. He was then released and told to beat it for home.

                                                    4. Document 4: War Industries Board, announcement, June 6, 1918, reprinted in The New York Times, June 7, 1918.

                                                      Be it Resolved, by the War Industries Board, That the following agreement reached as a result of several conferences between a committee of the board and the American Iron and Steel Institute, be and the same is hereby ratified, confirmed, and approved, to become effective at once: Whereas, A careful study of the sources of supply in connection with the present and rapidly increasing direct and indirect war requirements for iron and steel products has convinced the War Industries Board of the necessity for (1) a strict conservation of the available supply of iron and steel products, on the one hand, and (2) the expansion of existing sources and the development of new sources of supply of iron and steel products, on the other hand.

                                                    5. Document 5: President Woodrow Wilson, Address to the Senate, September 30, 1918.

                                                      Are we alone to ask and take the utmost that our women can give — service and sacrifice of every kind — and still say we do not see what title that gives them to stand by our sides in the guidance of the affairs of their nation and ours? We have made partners of the women in this war; shall we admit them only to a partnership of suffering and sacrifice and toil and not to a partnership of privilege and right?

                                                    6. Document 6: Billy Ireland, 'We Can't Digest the Scum,' Columbus Dispatch, March 4, 1919.

                                                      [Descriptive entry — no excerpted text in the source: a 1919 cartoon playing on the 'melting pot' image in reverse, depicting the United States as unable to 'digest' undesirable newcomers, reflecting postwar nativist and anti-radical sentiment.]

                                                    7. Document 7: Senator Warren G. Harding, address to the Home Market Club, Boston, May 14, 1920.

                                                      America's present need is not heroics, but healing; not nostrums, but normalcy; not revolution, but restoration; not agitation, but adjustment; not surgery, but serenity; not the dramatic, but the dispassionate; not experiment, but equipoise; not submergence in internationality, but sustainment in triumphant nationality. . . . The world needs to be reminded that all human ills are not curable by legislation, and that quantity of statutory enactment and excess of government offer no substitute for quality of citizenship.

                                                    Answer and explanation

                                                    Key: —

                                                    World War I fostered real but uneven and partly reversible change: it dramatically expanded federal power — criminalizing dissent (Docs 1, 3), directing industry (Doc 4) — and accelerated democratic claims, as Black Americans wielded Wilson's rhetoric against domestic racism (Doc 2) and women's wartime service propelled suffrage (Doc 5). Yet the postwar years showed the limits of that change: nativist backlash against immigrants and radicals (Doc 6) and Harding's 'return to normalcy' (Doc 7) deliberately dismantled wartime controls and deferred the era's promises of equality. The war's most lasting legacy was thus the precedent of an activist federal state, not a permanent social transformation.

                                                      LEQbarrons-2027-ch02-leq

                                                      Evaluate the extent to which changes in the American economy influenced patterns of internal migration in the United States in the period from 1865 to 1970.

                                                        Answer and explanation

                                                        Key: —

                                                        Economic change was the dominant driver of internal migration between 1865 and 1970: railroads and industrial jobs pulled immigrants and rural migrants to cities; depression-era collapse pushed Okies west and Black Southerners north; wartime production created the Great Migration's jobs and the Sunbelt's defense boom; and postwar prosperity, highways, and air conditioning made the Sunbelt's growth self-reinforcing. While racism, federal policy, and war itself shaped where people could go, the economy determined when and why they moved.

                                                          Which statement best captures the main argument the authors make in the passage?

                                                          1. A Puritan limits on trade kept New England's economy permanently behind the southern and middle colonies.
                                                          2. B New England under the Puritans reproduced the feudal manor system of medieval Europe, with estates passing from father to son over generations.
                                                          3. C As Puritan orthodoxy faded, Puritan work habits fused with freer markets into a market economy.
                                                          4. D New England's economy began to grow only after non-Puritan immigrants arrived in large numbers after 1640.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: C

                                                          The passage's thesis is the paradox: Puritan asceticism and the 'calling' bred hard work and wealth, and as strict religious orthodoxy faded, those work habits fused with market freedom — producing a market-oriented economy out of a moral one.

                                                          • A: The passage never claims New England was permanently behind the other regions. Its argument is developmental: the same moral economy that initially restrained markets later transformed into one. A claim about permanent regional inferiority contradicts the passage's thesis of growth.
                                                          • B: This confuses two different meanings of 'medieval.' The passage says Puritan economic life resembled the medieval moral economy — norms of just price and communal obligation — not that New England reproduced the feudal manor system. Puritan landholding was based on freehold family farms, not manorial estates with hereditary lordship.
                                                          • C: Correct. The passage's central paradox is that Puritan asceticism and the doctrine of the 'calling' bred disciplined, hard-working producers who accumulated wealth; then, as strict religious orthodoxy faded in the later 1600s, those ingrained work habits fused with freer market conditions. The result was a market-oriented economy that grew out of a moral one — the Puritan work ethic surviving its original religious container.
                                                          • D: The passage does not credit non-Puritan immigration after 1640 with starting growth. The economic transformation it describes was internal: Puritan work habits persisting and adapting as orthodoxy weakened, not an outside population arriving to build the economy. (In fact, large-scale non-Puritan immigration to New England came much later.)

                                                          QA findings

                                                          • minor · answer_tell — only one distractor uses absolute wording
                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch05-03

                                                          The Royal Proclamation of 1763 is best understood in the context of which broader development?

                                                          1. A Britain's move to give the colonies greater control over their own internal affairs.
                                                          2. B Britain's effort to consolidate imperial control over its North American empire.
                                                          3. C Britain's attempt to suppress revolutionary ideas already spreading in the colonies.
                                                          4. D Britain's shift from mercantilist regulation toward free-market capitalism.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: B

                                                          The proclamation was part of a post-1763 imperial reorganization: Britain sought tighter control — regulating western settlement, stationing troops, and extracting revenue through new taxes — to manage a vastly enlarged and debt-ridden empire.

                                                          • A: This is the exact opposite of the broader development. After 1763 Britain moved to reduce colonial self-direction — tightening customs enforcement, asserting Parliament's right to legislate for the colonies, and reserving decisions about western land to London. Greater colonial control over internal affairs was what colonists demanded, not what London offered.
                                                          • B: Correct. The Proclamation belongs to the post-1763 imperial reorganization: Britain had doubled its North American territory, inherited a massive war debt, and faced Pontiac's uprising. The response was consolidation — regulating western settlement, stationing a standing army in America (and then taxing colonists to pay for it), and extracting revenue through the Sugar, Stamp, and Townshend measures. The Proclamation was the first step in that tightening.
                                                          • C: A decade too early. In 1763 there was no revolutionary movement to suppress — the imperial crisis began with the Stamp Act in 1765, and independence talk came later still. The Proclamation was aimed at frontier stability and imperial economy, not at silencing colonial radicals who did not yet exist.
                                                          • D: Britain did not move toward free-market capitalism in 1763; it doubled down on mercantilism. The Navigation Acts stayed in force and enforcement tightened, and the whole revenue program of the 1760s assumed the empire existed for the mother country's economic benefit. Adam Smith would not publish The Wealth of Nations until 1776.

                                                          QA findings

                                                          • major · explanation_consistency — distractor explanation appears to label itself correct
                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch05-09

                                                          Americans who shared Washington's outlook in this letter would most likely have taken which of the following later positions?

                                                          1. A They would have urged the United States to honor the 1778 alliance by joining France's war against Britain in 1793.
                                                          2. B They would have opposed chartering the Bank of the United States in 1791.
                                                          3. C They would have supported ratification of the Constitution in 1787–1788.
                                                          4. D They would have opposed the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: C

                                                          Washington's remedy for a feeble confederation was a stronger national government — the position that carried the Philadelphia Convention and the ratification fight. He became the Constitution's most prestigious supporter and the first president under it.

                                                          • A: Washington did the opposite. In 1793, when France's war with Britain raised the question of honoring the 1778 alliance, Washington issued the Proclamation of Neutrality, keeping the United States out of the war. Someone sharing his outlook would have backed neutrality, not intervention for France.
                                                          • B: Washington signed the Bank bill into law in 1791, after Hamilton persuaded him it was constitutional. Supporters of Washington's strong-government outlook backed the Bank of the United States; opposition to it came from Jefferson and Madison.
                                                          • C: Correct. Washington's letter concludes that the Confederation's weakness can only be cured by a government with real, coercive national power — the exact argument for the Constitution. He presided over the Philadelphia Convention, lent his prestige to ratification, and became the first president under the new system. Anyone sharing this letter's outlook would have been a Federalist for ratification in 1787–88.
                                                          • D: The Alien and Sedition Acts (1798) were supported by the Federalist camp — the political heirs of Washington's strong-national-government outlook — and opposed by Jeffersonian Republicans. Someone sharing Washington's outlook would have backed, not opposed, measures strengthening federal authority.

                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch06-01

                                                          The argument this essay makes grew most directly out of which of the following developments?

                                                          1. A The rise of wage labor, which drew thousands of young women into mills and factories where their work was stigmatized as degrading.
                                                          2. B The westward movement of settlers beyond the Appalachian Mountains.
                                                          3. C The religious revivals of the Second Great Awakening.
                                                          4. D The political battles over the Bank of the United States.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: A

                                                          The Lowell Offering was written by the young women working in the Massachusetts textile mills of the 1840s. The essay's roll call of princesses, Lucretia, Penelope, and Queen Charlotte — all doing manual work — answers the specific stigma these wage-earning women faced: that physical labor was 'derogatory to a lady's dignity.' The argument is a defense of mill women's respectability, rooted in the new experience of female wage labor.

                                                          • A: Correct. The Lowell Offering was written in the 1840s by the young women tending power looms in Lowell's textile mills — the 'mill girls' recruited from New England farms. They faced a real social stigma: that physical wage labor was 'derogatory to a lady's dignity.' The essay's defense is built for that audience and that insult — its roll call of princesses drawing water, Lucretia spinning among her attendants, Penelope weaving, and Queen Charlotte doing manual work argues that labor has always been compatible with feminine dignity. The argument exists because thousands of young women had entered wage labor and needed to answer the charge that doing so degraded them.
                                                          • B: The westward movement beyond the Appalachians had nothing to do with this essay. The mill girls were New England farm daughters who went to work in Massachusetts factory towns, not settlers heading west; the essay is about factory work and its dignity, not the frontier.
                                                          • C: The Second Great Awakening was a Protestant religious revival, not the development behind this essay. Although it overlapped in time, the essay's subject is the dignity of women's manual wage labor in the mills — an economic and social defense — not revival religion or conversion.
                                                          • D: The political battles over the Bank of the United States (Jackson's war on the Bank, 1832–36) were a fight over federal economic power, entirely unrelated to a mill women's literary defense of factory work. Nothing in the essay touches banking, the national bank, or federal finance.

                                                          QA findings

                                                          • major · answer_tell — keyed answer is uniquely and substantially longest
                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch06-03

                                                          The Lowell Offering most directly reflects which of the following broader developments?

                                                          1. A The Arts and Crafts movement's revival of traditional artisan methods.
                                                          2. B The entry of women into clerical office jobs as typists and receptionists.
                                                          3. C The shift from semi-subsistence farming to production for distant markets.
                                                          4. D A campaign to have women's domestic work formally counted as paid labor.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: C

                                                          The mill girls were part of the market revolution: Americans shifting from semi-subsistence farming to producing goods for distant markets, whether in factories or through the putting-out system of home piecework.

                                                          • A: The Arts and Crafts movement was a late-nineteenth-century reaction against industrialization (1870s onward) that romanticized hand craftsmanship. The Lowell Offering belongs to the opposite moment — the early industrial era, when factory production was new and its defenders were arguing for the dignity of mill work.
                                                          • B: Women's entry into clerical office work — typists, stenographers, receptionists — came later in the nineteenth century, with the spread of the typewriter and the corporate office. The Offering's authors were factory operatives, not office workers.
                                                          • C: Correct. The mill girls were products of the market revolution: the early-nineteenth-century transformation in which Americans shifted from semi-subsistence farming toward producing goods for distant markets. Some did it in factories like Lowell's; others through the putting-out system of home piecework. The Offering is a cultural artifact of that economic transformation.
                                                          • D: No such campaign existed in the 1840s, and the essay does not argue for it. The Offering defends the dignity of women's wage labor in the mills; it does not ask that unpaid domestic work be reclassified as paid labor.

                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch06-07

                                                          Finney's theology, as described in the passage, most directly supported which of the following?

                                                          1. A A return to strict Calvinist church discipline and the doctrine of the elect.
                                                          2. B The era's reform movements, since the belief that any sinner could choose conversion implied that society itself could be perfected.
                                                          3. C The rapid growth of Catholic immigration to American cities.
                                                          4. D The movement to disestablish state-supported churches.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: B

                                                          Finney's claim that even 'harlots, and drunkards, infidels' could be 'awakened and converted' rejected predestination in favor of human agency: sinners choose to repent. That same agency underwrote the perfectionist reform impulse of the 1830s–1840s — temperance, abolition, moral reform — because if individuals could perfect themselves, society could be perfected too.

                                                          • A: Finney broke with strict Calvinism rather than returning to it. His revivalism rejected predestination and the doctrine of the elect: his whole point was that any sinner — 'harlots, and drunkards, infidels' — could choose to repent and be converted. Church discipline of the old Calvinist sort was precisely what his theology of free will moved away from.
                                                          • B: Correct. Finney's theology rested on human agency: sinners are not predestined but can choose conversion, and revivals are the product of human effort as much as divine grace. If even the most 'abandoned' sinner could be transformed by choice, then society itself could be perfected by concerted moral effort — the perfectionist logic that powered the era's reform movements: temperance, abolition, moral reform, women's rights.
                                                          • C: Catholic immigration to American cities was driven by Irish and German immigration, not by Finney's theology. Finney was a Presbyterian-turned-revivalist Protestant whose movement was, if anything, culturally hostile to Catholicism; his theology did not cause or support Catholic growth.
                                                          • D: Disestablishment of state-supported churches was largely complete before Finney's peak — Massachusetts, the last state with an established church, disestablished in 1833. Finney's theology of conversion and moral agency was about revival and reform, not about the legal separation of church and state.

                                                          QA findings

                                                          • major · answer_tell — keyed answer is uniquely and substantially longest
                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch08-03

                                                          Which of the following shared the Dawes Act's underlying goal for the future of Native peoples?

                                                          1. A The Ghost Dance movement's spiritual revival.
                                                          2. B The federal Indian boarding schools that erased Native languages.
                                                          3. C The Indian Reorganization Act's restoration of tribal governments.
                                                          4. D The American Indian Movement's 1960s activism.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: B

                                                          Off-reservation boarding schools (e.g., Carlisle) cut children's hair, banned Native languages, imposed English names and vocational training — the same assimilationist logic as allotment: erase tribal identity by remaking the individual. The Indian Reorganization Act (1934) reversed this; AIM (1968) opposed it.

                                                          • A: The Ghost Dance was Native spiritual resistance to assimilation, not an expression of it. The 1890 movement promised the disappearance of whites and the return of the buffalo — a vision of deliverance from the very policies the Dawes Act embodied. It shared nothing with allotment's goal.
                                                          • B: Correct. The off-reservation boarding schools — Carlisle being the famous example — pursued the same goal as allotment by different means: erase tribal identity by remaking the individual. Children had their hair cut, were forbidden to speak Native languages, were given English names, and were trained for manual labor. Allotment attacked tribalism through land; the schools attacked it through children. Both were instruments of forced assimilation.
                                                          • C: The Indian Reorganization Act (1934) reversed the Dawes Act's goal, not shared it. The IRA ended allotment, restored the remaining land base, and encouraged tribal governments — the New Deal's repudiation of assimilation.
                                                          • D: The American Indian Movement (founded 1968) opposed assimilationist policy, not continued it. AIM's activism — from the Trail of Broken Treaties to Wounded Knee — demanded treaty rights and tribal sovereignty, the opposite of the Dawes Act's program of dissolving tribes into individual landowners.

                                                          • No findings
                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch08-07

                                                          Which later movement most fully carried forward the Grange's political and economic agenda?

                                                          1. A The Congress of Industrial Organizations' labor organizing.
                                                          2. B The Populist Party's 1890s farmer-labor platform.
                                                          3. C The NAACP's civil-rights litigation strategy.
                                                          4. D The 1960s New Left student movement.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: B

                                                          The Populist (People's) Party of the 1890s absorbed the Granger program — railroad regulation, an income tax, free coinage of silver, subtreasury farm loans — and carried it into national politics with the 1892 Omaha Platform.

                                                          • A: The Congress of Industrial Organizations was a 1930s industrial-labor movement organizing factory workers — a different century, a different constituency, and a labor rather than agrarian program. It did not inherit the Grange's farmer-focused agenda of railroad regulation and farm credit.
                                                          • B: Correct. The Populist (People's) Party of the 1890s absorbed the Granger program wholesale — railroad regulation, a graduated income tax, free coinage of silver, and the subtreasury plan for farm loans — and carried it into national politics in the 1892 Omaha Platform. Populism was the Grange's political heir.
                                                          • C: The NAACP's civil-rights litigation strategy addressed racial discrimination through the courts — a different cause, a different method, a different constituency. It carried forward no part of the Grange's agrarian economic agenda.
                                                          • D: The 1960s New Left was a student movement focused on civil rights, the Vietnam War, and university reform — generationally and programmatically distant from the Grange's farmer politics of railroad rates and farm credit.

                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch08-08

                                                          [Image description: Frederick Burr Opper, 'Just as dangerous now as then,' 1883. A cartoon drawing a parallel between the perils the Pilgrims faced arriving in seventeenth-century America and the perils facing immigrants arriving in the 1880s.] The cartoon's point is which of the following?

                                                          1. A The 'new immigrants' of eastern and southern Europe were as dangerous to America as Native peoples had been to the Pilgrims.
                                                          2. B America was filling up, and new immigrants would displace native-born Americans just as the Pilgrims displaced Native peoples.
                                                          3. C The immigrant stream contained radicals, anarchists, and criminals who threatened the nation.
                                                          4. D Newly arrived immigrants faced a gauntlet of exploitation and hardship, just as the Pilgrims had in the 1600s.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: D

                                                          Unlike most nativist cartoons of the era, Opper's is sympathetic: it parallels the Pilgrims' seventeenth-century hardships with the gauntlet facing 1880s immigrants — swindling money-changers, baggage thieves, slum landlords, and exploitative employers.

                                                          • A: This misreads the cartoon's sympathy. Opper's cartoon is pro-immigrant: it parallels the Pilgrims' hardships with those of 1880s immigrants to argue that the newcomers deserve the same understanding the Pilgrims receive. It does not portray immigrants as dangerous — that was the nativist position the cartoon answers.
                                                          • B: The cartoon is not about immigrants displacing native-born Americans. Its parallel runs the other way: just as the Pilgrims faced a gauntlet of perils arriving in the 1600s, so do today's immigrants. The subject is what immigrants endure, not whom they displace.
                                                          • C: Radicals and anarchists are not the cartoon's subject. Opper shows the gauntlet facing ordinary immigrants — swindling money-changers, baggage thieves, slum landlords, exploitative employers — not a parade of political extremists threatening the nation.
                                                          • D: Correct. Unusually for its nativist era, Opper's 1883 cartoon is sympathetic: it draws a parallel between the perils the Pilgrims faced arriving in seventeenth-century America and the gauntlet facing immigrants in the 1880s — exploitation by money-changers, thieves, landlords, and employers. The point is that the newcomers' hardships mirror the nation's own founding story and deserve the same respect.

                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch09-01

                                                          [Image description: Victor Gillam, 'Overlooked — or The Folly of Foreign Missions,' Judge magazine, 1895. A Protestant missionary peers through a telescope toward distant lands, oblivious to impoverished, suffering figures huddled at his feet.] The cartoonist's point of view is which of the following?

                                                          1. A Missionaries fixated on overseas converts while ignoring poverty at home.
                                                          2. B Open immigration was destabilizing the American economy.
                                                          3. C The United States should embrace overseas imperialism.
                                                          4. D The widening gap between rich and poor was creating a revolutionary situation.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: A

                                                          The cartoon shows a missionary peering through a telescope at distant lands while ragged, suffering poor crowd unnoticed at his feet — a critique of churches spending energy on foreign converts while ignoring poverty in American cities.

                                                          • A: Correct. Gillam's 1895 cartoon shows a Protestant missionary peering through a telescope toward distant lands, oblivious to the ragged, suffering poor huddled at his feet. The title says it plainly: 'The Folly of Foreign Missions.' The cartoonist's point is one of misplaced priorities — churches spending money and energy converting people overseas while ignoring the poverty, sweatshops, and slums of American cities right in front of them.
                                                          • B: Immigration is not the cartoon's subject. The figures at the missionary's feet represent the urban poor generally, and the critique is aimed at the churches' priorities — foreign missions versus domestic poverty — not at whether immigration was destabilizing the economy.
                                                          • C: The cartoon argues against overseas ventures, not for them. Its whole point is that American churches should turn their attention homeward instead of gazing abroad; embracing overseas imperialism would be the telescope's direction, which the cartoonist calls folly.
                                                          • D: The cartoon warns about neglected poverty, not about revolution. Nothing in the image suggests the poor are about to rise up; the critique is moral — the churches' indifference — not a prediction of class revolution.

                                                          • No findings
                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch09-08

                                                          The changes Cohen describes were later reinforced by which of the following?

                                                          1. A Senator Joseph McCarthy's anti-Communist crusade and loyalty investigations of the 1950s.
                                                          2. B President Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs of the 1960s.
                                                          3. C President Ronald Reagan's domestic agenda of the 1980s.
                                                          4. D The 1990s 'Contract with America.'
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: B

                                                          LBJ's Great Society — the Civil Rights Acts, the War on Poverty, Medicare/Medicaid — extended the New Deal's premise of federal responsibility for welfare and economic security into the 1960s.

                                                          • A: McCarthy's anti-Communist crusade attacked the left and purged suspected subversives from government and unions — it weakened the labor-left coalition and chilled reform, rather than reinforcing the welfare state and union acceptance Cohen describes.
                                                          • B: Correct. Lyndon Johnson's Great Society — the Civil Rights Acts, the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid — extended the New Deal's premise into the 1960s: that the federal government bears responsibility for citizens' welfare and economic security. It was the second great wave of the transformation Cohen traces.
                                                          • C: Reagan's domestic agenda moved in the opposite direction: cutting domestic programs, deregulating, and declaring that government was the problem. It was an assault on the New Deal order, not a reinforcement of it.
                                                          • D: The 1994 'Contract with America' sought to shrink the federal government — welfare reform, balanced budgets, devolution. Like Reaganism, it aimed to roll back the welfare-state premises Cohen describes, not reinforce them.

                                                          QA findings

                                                          • No findings
                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch09-09

                                                          Black's opinion in Korematsu rejected which of the following arguments?

                                                          1. A That Congress had given the military legal authority to issue the exclusion orders.
                                                          2. B That fears of a West Coast invasion were sincerely held by military commanders.
                                                          3. C That the exclusion order was driven by racial prejudice rather than genuine military necessity.
                                                          4. D That courts should defer to military judgments during wartime.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: C

                                                          Black's majority opinion insisted the exclusion rested 'not on racial hostility but on wartime military judgments about invasion fears and security,' expressly rejecting the claim — pressed by Korematsu and the dissenters — that the policy was racial prejudice dressed up as military necessity. The opinion accepted congressional authorization, took invasion fears as sincere, and deferred to the military on all other points.

                                                          • A: Black did not reject this argument — he relied on it. His opinion accepts that Congress had empowered the military to issue the exclusion orders; congressional authorization is part of the foundation his reasoning stands on, not a claim he dismisses.
                                                          • B: Black did not reject the sincerity of invasion fears — he took them as genuine. His opinion treats the military commanders' fears of a West Coast invasion as sincerely held judgments, which is precisely why he defers to them.
                                                          • C: Correct. Black's majority opinion insists the exclusion rested 'not on racial hostility but on wartime military judgments about invasion fears and security' — expressly rejecting the argument, pressed by Korematsu and the dissenters (notably Justice Murphy), that the policy was racial prejudice dressed up as military necessity. The opinion's central move is to reclassify a race-based order as a security measure.
                                                          • D: Black did not reject deference to the military — he embraced it. His opinion holds that courts must defer to military judgments during wartime, which is the doctrinal basis for upholding the exclusion orders.

                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch10-01

                                                          [Image description: Herblock, 'Have a care, sir,' Washington Post, 1954. Senator Joseph McCarthy on the left, menacing and aggressive; President Dwight D. Eisenhower on the right, offering only a mild rebuke.] The cartoon's point is which of the following?

                                                          1. A McCarthy and Eisenhower cooperated effectively to halt the spread of Communism at home.
                                                          2. B McCarthy went too far when he accused Eisenhower himself of Communist sympathies.
                                                          3. C McCarthy wisely guarded the nation while Eisenhower blindly ignored security threats.
                                                          4. D Eisenhower's public criticisms of McCarthy's crusade were feeble and inadequate.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: D

                                                          Herblock's cartoon shows Eisenhower offering only a meek 'Have a care, sir' while McCarthy brandishes his smear tactics — criticizing the president for refusing to confront McCarthyism directly even as he found the senator's methods 'reprehensible.'

                                                          • A: The cartoon shows no such cooperation. Herblock draws McCarthy as menacing and aggressive while Eisenhower offers only a mild 'Have a care, sir' — the image is a rebuke of the president's passivity, not a celebration of teamwork against Communism.
                                                          • B: McCarthy never accused Eisenhower himself of Communist sympathies — his targets were the State Department, the Army, alleged spies, and 'fellow travelers.' The cartoon's complaint is different: not that McCarthy attacked the president, but that the president would not attack McCarthy.
                                                          • C: Herblock was McCarthy's fiercest cartoonist critic; the drawing condemns the senator, not praises him. The menacing figure on the left is the villain of the image, and the mild figure on the right is being criticized for tolerating him — the opposite of praising McCarthy's vigilance.
                                                          • D: Correct. Herblock's 1954 cartoon shows a menacing, aggressive McCarthy beside an Eisenhower who offers only a meek 'Have a care, sir.' The point is the inadequacy of the president's response: Eisenhower privately found McCarthy's methods reprehensible but refused to confront him publicly, and Herblock is indicting that refusal — the feebleness of a mild rebuke against a demagogue's smear tactics.

                                                          • major · explanation_consistency — distractor explanation appears to label itself correct
                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch10-05

                                                          Savio's speech best reflects which broader trend of the 1960s?

                                                          1. A Conservatives mobilized against juvenile delinquency and the decline of the traditional family.
                                                          2. B Artists and writers withdrew from politics into abstract expression.
                                                          3. C Activists on the left charged liberals with failing to transform the status quo.
                                                          4. D Working-class militants rebelled against complacent union leadership.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: C

                                                          The New Left — veterans of Freedom Summer and campus activism — attacked Cold War liberalism from the left, arguing that the Warren Court and the Great Society, for all their achievements, left racial and economic structures fundamentally untransformed.

                                                          • A: Conservative mobilization against delinquency and family decline was the right's story in the 1960s, not Savio's. The Free Speech Movement and the New Left attacked liberal institutions from the left; conservatives were their opponents, not their trend.
                                                          • B: Artists withdrawing from politics into abstraction describes the 1950s abstract expressionists, not the 1960s activists. Savio's generation did the opposite — it plunged into politics, from campus protests to Freedom Summer.
                                                          • C: Correct. Savio's speech exemplifies the New Left's defining move: charging Cold War liberals with failing to transform the status quo. Veterans of Freedom Summer and campus activism argued that for all the Warren Court's rulings and the Great Society's programs, racial and economic structures remained fundamentally untransformed — liberalism managed the system rather than remaking it.
                                                          • D: Working-class rebellion against union leadership describes rank-and-file labor militancy, not the student Free Speech Movement. Savio's constituency was university students, and his target was the university bureaucracy — a campus revolt, not a shop-floor one.

                                                          QA findings

                                                          • major · explanation_consistency — distractor explanation appears to label itself correct
                                                          MCQbarrons-2027-ch11-02

                                                          Which generalization about the Contract with America's aftermath is best supported?

                                                          1. A Republicans were shut out of the House, Senate, and presidency for a decade afterward.
                                                          2. B Republicans successfully dismantled the core programs of Lyndon Johnson's Great Society.
                                                          3. C Even as Republicans denounced 'big government,' the federal government kept growing.
                                                          4. D Large numbers of House Republicans defected to the Democratic Party in protest.
                                                          Answer and explanation

                                                          Key: C

                                                          Despite the 1994 rhetoric, federal spending and the scope of government kept growing through the 1990s and 2000s — popular programs (Social Security, Medicare) proved politically untouchable, and even Republican administrations expanded the state.

                                                          • A: Republicans were not shut out — they won both the House and the Senate in 1994 and held Congress for most of the next decade. This describes the opposite of what happened.
                                                          • B: The core Great Society programs survived the 1994 revolution intact. Medicare, Medicaid, and federal education and antipoverty programs were not dismantled — they proved politically untouchable, and Republicans learned that attacking popular entitlements carried electoral costs (as the 1995–96 government shutdowns showed).
                                                          • C: Correct. The irony of the post-1994 era is that for all the Contract's denunciations of 'big government,' the federal government kept growing — through the late 1990s and 2000s, under both parties. Popular programs like Social Security and Medicare could not be touched politically, and even Republican administrations expanded the state (the prescription-drug benefit, homeland security, education mandates). Rhetoric shrank government; budgets did not.
                                                          • D: No such defection occurred. House Republicans did not cross to the Democratic Party in protest after 1994 — the Republican majority held together, and party-switching in this era ran the other direction (southern conservatives joining the GOP).

When in health, the laborer shall work ten hours during the day in the summer, and nine hours during the day in winter . . . he shall obey all proper orders of his employer or his agent. . . . Failure to obey reasonable orders, neglect of duty, and leaving home without permission will be deemed disobedience; impudence, swearing, or indecent language to or in the presence of the employer, his family or agent . . . shall be deemed disobedience.

                                                            4. Document 4: 'Selling a Freeman to Pay His Fine at Monticello, Florida,' Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper, January 19, 1867.

                                                              [Image description: An engraving showing a Black freedman being auctioned on a platform before a crowd of white bidders in Monticello, Florida — sold into labor to satisfy a fine imposed under the South's vagrancy laws.]

                                                            5. Document 5: Petition to U.S. Congress, South Carolina Colored People's Convention, November 1865.

                                                              We simply desire that we shall be recognized as men; that we have no obstructions placed in our way; that the same laws which govern white men shall direct colored men; that we have the right of trial by a jury of our peers, that schools be opened or established for our children; that we be permitted to acquire homesteads for ourselves and children; that we be dealt with as others, in equity and justice. . . . We trust the day will not be distant when you will acknowledge that by our rapid progress in moral, social, religious and intellectual development that you will cheerfully accord to us the high commendation that we are worthy, with you, to enjoy all political emoluments.

                                                            6. Document 6: Speech, Samuel J. Tilden, leader of the Democratic Party, New York, 1868.

                                                              [The Republican Party] resolved to make the black race the governing power in those States, and by means of them to bring into Congress twenty senators and fifty representatives practically appointed by itself in Washington. . . . Nor is there the slightest doubt that the paramount object and motive of the Republican party is by these means to secure itself against a reaction of opinion adverse to it in our great populous Northern commonwealths.

                                                            7. Document 7: Thaddeus Stevens, speech in Congress, January 3, 1867.

                                                              We have broken the material shackles of four million slaves. We have unchained them from the stake so as to allow them locomotion, provided they do not walk in paths which are trod by white men. . . . What is negro equality, about which so much is said by knaves and some of which is believed by men who are not fools? It means, as understood by honest Republicans, just this much, and no more: every man, no matter what his race or colour; every earthly being who has an immortal soul, has an equal right to justice, honesty, and fair play with every other man; and the law should secure him those rights. The same law, which condemns or acquits an African, should condemn or acquit a white man.

                                                            Answer and explanation

                                                            Key: —

                                                            The Johnson–Congress collision was caused most fundamentally by an irreconcilable disagreement over what emancipation required: southern Black Codes restoring near-slavery (Docs 2, 3, 4) convinced congressional Republicans that freedom demanded federal guarantees of civil and political equality (Doc 7), a demand freedpeople themselves pressed on Congress (Doc 5), while Johnson's commitment to rapid, lenient restoration in Lincoln's 'malice toward none' spirit (Doc 1) led him to defend the southern states instead. Partisan calculations about a new Black Republican electorate (Doc 6) intensified the fight but did not create it — the moral and constitutional stakes were primary.

                                                              • No findings
                                                              LEQbarrons-2027-pt1-leq

                                                              The Populist movement, the Progressive movement, and the Civil Rights Movement were among the major reform movements in the United States between 1877 and 1970. Explain how reform movements influenced American society and government in the period from 1877 to 1970.

                                                                Answer and explanation

                                                                Key: —

                                                                Reform movements between 1877 and 1970 progressively expanded the federal government's responsibilities and ordinary Americans' political power: Populists, though electorally defeated, injected demands — graduated income taxation, direct election of senators, railroad regulation — that Progressives later enacted into law; Progressives built the modern regulatory state (antitrust, food and drug safety, the Federal Reserve) and democratized politics through direct primaries and the initiative; and the civil rights movement, through nonviolent direct action and federal legislation, finally extended the franchise and legal equality to Black Americans, making the federal government the guarantor of civil rights. Each movement thus left government larger, more interventionist, and more democratically accountable than it found it.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-01

                                                                  Garrison's rhetoric in the passage — addressing readers as 'free people of color' and fellow citizens — reflects which abolitionist strategy?

                                                                  1. A Organizing armed slave rebellions across the South.
                                                                  2. B Working quietly through the established national political parties.
                                                                  3. C Moral suasion: appealing to conscience and American ideals to demand immediate change.
                                                                  4. D Campaigning for gradual, compensated emancipation.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: C

                                                                  Garrison's Liberator practiced moral suasion: he addressed free Black readers as citizens, insisted their treatment as 'aliens and brutes' proved only 'the bitterness and blindness of prejudice,' and demanded readers confront slavery as a sin against American ideals — aiming to convert hearts rather than bargain through parties or wait for gradual schemes.

                                                                  • A: Garrison was a pacifist who rejected violence as a means — he denounced slave rebellions and insisted slavery must end through moral conversion, not bloodshed. Organizing armed rebellions was the opposite of his strategy.
                                                                  • B: Garrison rejected working through the established parties, which he saw as corrupted by compromises with slavery ('no union with slaveholders'). The Liberator's whole method was agitation outside party politics, not quiet work within it.
                                                                  • C: Correct. Garrison's Liberator practiced moral suasion: addressing free Black readers as 'free people of color' and fellow citizens, insisting their degradation proved only 'the bitterness and blindness of prejudice,' and demanding that readers confront slavery as a sin against American ideals. The strategy aimed to convert hearts and consciences — to make slavery morally intolerable — rather than to bargain politically.
                                                                  • D: Gradual, compensated emancipation was the position of moderates and colonizationists, not Garrison's. He demanded immediate, uncompensated emancipation — 'immediate' was in the Liberator's masthead logic — and denounced gradualism as compromise with sin.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-04

                                                                  [Image description: two maps of North America east of the Mississippi — the first showing overlapping colonial-era state claims stretching to the Mississippi River, the second showing those claims ceded and the Old Northwest organized as a national domain.] The differences between the maps illustrate which of the following?

                                                                  1. A The Confederation government's resolution of competing western land claims.
                                                                  2. B Territorial changes imposed by the treaty ending the French and Indian War.
                                                                  3. C The changing legal status of slavery in newly acquired American territories.
                                                                  4. D The effects of the Quasi-War with France on western land claims.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: A

                                                                  The two maps show the Old Northwest before and after the Confederation period: states ceded their western claims, creating a national domain — the Confederation Congress's signal achievement, enabling the Land Ordinance of 1785 and Northwest Ordinance of 1787.

                                                                  • A: Correct. The two maps show the Old Northwest before and after the Confederation period: in the first, states like Virginia and Connecticut assert overlapping claims stretching to the Mississippi; in the second, those claims have been ceded to create a national domain. Getting the states to surrender their western claims was the Confederation government's signal achievement — it made the Land Ordinance of 1785 and the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 possible.
                                                                  • B: The treaty ending the French and Indian War (1763) transferred French and Spanish claims among European empires — it did not involve American states ceding overlapping claims to a national government, which did not yet exist. Wrong treaty, wrong century's logic.
                                                                  • C: The maps show who owned the land, not the legal status of slavery within it. Slavery's status in the Northwest came from the Northwest Ordinance's Article 6, but the map-to-map change is about state cessions creating a national domain, not about slavery law.
                                                                  • D: The Quasi-War (1798) was an undeclared naval conflict with France that had no effect on western land claims. It belongs to the Adams administration's foreign crises, not to the Confederation's land settlement.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-11

                                                                  The Spanish accommodation Calloway describes was caused most directly by which of the following?

                                                                  1. A The Pueblo Revolt of 1680, which expelled the Spanish from New Mexico for twelve years.
                                                                  2. B The arrival of French missionaries promoting a gentler approach.
                                                                  3. C The discovery of silver deposits in New Mexico.
                                                                  4. D A royal decree from Madrid ordering religious toleration in the colonies.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: A

                                                                  Pope's coordinated 1680 rising killed friars, destroyed Catholic ritual objects, and drove the Spanish out for twelve years. When the Spanish reconquered New Mexico, they had learned the lesson: friars who once tried to wipe out every Native practice now often tolerated Pueblo religion, because renewed repression risked another revolt.

                                                                  • A: Correct. The Spanish accommodation Calloway describes was a lesson learned the hard way: in 1680, Popé — a Tewa religious leader from San Juan — coordinated a Pueblo rising that killed friars who had tried to crush Native religion, destroyed Catholic ritual objects, and expelled the Spanish from New Mexico for twelve years. When the Spanish reconquered the region in the 1690s, friars who had once tried to wipe out every Native practice now often tolerated Pueblo religion — because the revolt had taught them that severity was unsustainable.
                                                                  • B: No French missionaries operated in New Mexico in this era — New Mexico was Spanish territory, far from French Louisiana's sphere. The gentler approach came from Spanish friars chastened by the revolt, not from French newcomers.
                                                                  • C: No silver discovery in New Mexico drove this change. New Mexico's value to Spain was strategic and missionary, not mineral — the great silver strikes were in Mexico and the Andes. The cause of the policy shift was military and political: the revolt.
                                                                  • D: No royal decree from Madrid ordered religious toleration in the colonies. The accommodation was pragmatic and local — friars and officials in New Mexico adjusting after the reconquest — not a metropolitan policy directive.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-12

                                                                  The excerpt suggests that Pueblo societies most commonly responded to the Spanish presence by doing which of the following?

                                                                  1. A They rapidly abandoned their traditions for Spanish culture.
                                                                  2. B They adopted selected Spanish elements while preserving cultural autonomy.
                                                                  3. C They rejected Spanish culture but accepted Spanish political institutions.
                                                                  4. D They mastered Spanish military technology and turned it against the Spanish.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: B

                                                                  Luis's blended dress — animal skins and palm-shell bands alongside rosary and silver cross — exemplifies selective adaptation: Pueblos took up Catholic symbols while preserving core Native practices and autonomy, neither total assimilation nor total rejection.

                                                                  • A: The Pueblos did not rapidly abandon their traditions — they preserved their core religious and social practices through the entire colonial period, reviving them openly after the 1680 revolt. The excerpt's whole point is cultural persistence, not surrender.
                                                                  • B: Correct. The excerpt's example — Luis's blended dress, animal skins and palm-shell bands worn alongside a rosary and silver cross — shows the Pueblo pattern: adopting selected Spanish elements (Catholic symbols, some material goods) while preserving cultural autonomy and core Native practices. Neither total assimilation nor total rejection, but strategic selection.
                                                                  • C: The Pueblos did not accept Spanish political institutions while rejecting the culture — they preserved their own village governance and religious life, and repeatedly resisted Spanish authority itself (most decisively in 1680). The selection ran the other way: cultural borrowing without political submission.
                                                                  • D: The Pueblos did not defeat the Spanish with superior Spanish military technology — they won in 1680 through coordinated surprise across dozens of villages, seizing the moment when Spanish forces were dispersed. Military technology was not their path; organization and timing were.

                                                                  Which of the following positions most closely parallels the anti-intervention stance of the cartoon?

                                                                  1. A William Randolph Hearst's pro-war yellow journalism in 1898.
                                                                  2. B The Abraham Lincoln Brigade's support for intervening in the Spanish Civil War.
                                                                  3. C Dean Acheson's support for U.S. intervention in Korea in 1950.
                                                                  4. D Martin Luther King Jr.'s opposition to the Vietnam War in 1967.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: D

                                                                  Both the 1936 isolationists and King's 1967 antiwar position opposed American military entanglement abroad — the parallel is opposition to intervention, not support for it.

                                                                  • A: Hearst's yellow journalism in 1898 clamored for war with Spain — the opposite of the cartoon's anti-intervention stance. Hearst wanted America in; the cartoon wants America out.
                                                                  • B: The Abraham Lincoln Brigade fought in the Spanish Civil War — Americans volunteering to intervene against Franco. That is interventionism in its most personal form, the reverse of the cartoon's position.
                                                                  • C: Dean Acheson, as Truman's Secretary of State, was the architect of intervention in Korea in 1950 — the containment doctrine in action. His position is the anti-isolationist one.
                                                                  • D: Correct. Both the 1936 isolationists and Martin Luther King Jr.'s 1967 opposition to the Vietnam War took the same structural position: against American military entanglement abroad. The parallel is the stance toward intervention — stay out — across three decades and very different causes.

                                                                  Truman's argument most directly reflects which long-running continuity in American history?

                                                                  1. A Debates over the balance of power between Congress and the president.
                                                                  2. B Debates over using military force in unstable regions.
                                                                  3. C Debates over the United States' proper role in world affairs.
                                                                  4. D Debates over the proper role of political parties.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: C

                                                                  From Washington's Farewell Address through the League of Nations fight to Cold War internationalism, Americans have continuously debated how deeply the U.S. should engage the world — Truman's 1947 address is a landmark in that debate.

                                                                  • A: The address is not about Congress versus the president — Truman was asking Congress for action, not contesting its power. The separation-of-powers debate is a different continuity.

                                                                  • C: Correct. From Washington's Farewell Address through the League of Nations fight to Cold War internationalism, Americans have continuously debated how deeply the United States should engage the world — isolation versus intervention, entanglement versus detachment. Truman's 1947 address is a landmark in that permanent debate: the moment non-entanglement gave way to global containment.
                                                                  • D: The proper role of political parties is not at issue in the address. Truman's argument concerns America's role in the world, not party organization or function.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-21

                                                                  Calhoun's constitutional argument here most closely resembles which earlier debate?

                                                                  1. A Whether enslaved people should be counted in the census for purposes of representation.
                                                                  2. B Whether the Constitution authorized the Louisiana Purchase.
                                                                  3. C Whether states should disestablish the Episcopal Church.
                                                                  4. D Whether to replace the Articles of Confederation with the Constitution.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: D

                                                                  Calhoun's warning against a 'great consolidated government, with unlimited powers' that would 'divest the States, in reality, of all their rights' echoes the Anti-Federalists, who used strikingly similar states'-rights language against ratifying the Constitution — in both debates the power of the states versus the center was the issue.

                                                                  • A: Whether enslaved people counted in the census for representation was settled by the three-fifths compromise — a bargaining outcome about apportionment, not a debate over consolidated versus federal government power.
                                                                  • B: Whether the Constitution authorized the Louisiana Purchase was a debate about implied executive power (Jefferson's own scruples), not about the Anti-Federalist fear of consolidated government swallowing the states.
                                                                  • C: Disestablishing the Episcopal Church was a state-level religious-freedom question, unrelated to Calhoun's argument about the division of sovereignty between the general and state governments.
                                                                  • D: Correct. Calhoun's warning against a 'great consolidated government, with unlimited powers' that would 'divest the States, in reality, of all their rights' echoes the Anti-Federalists, who used strikingly similar states'-rights language against ratifying the Constitution in 1787–88. In both debates the fear is the same: that national power will swallow the states.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-22

                                                                  Calhoun's language of 'protest' against federal overreach most closely echoes the language of which earlier group?

                                                                  1. A Jackson's supporters denouncing the 'corrupt bargain' of 1824.
                                                                  2. B New England Federalists protesting the War of 1812.
                                                                  3. C The Jefferson administration confronting the Barbary pirates.
                                                                  4. D Daniel Shays's rebels protesting Massachusetts fiscal policy.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: B

                                                                  The Hartford Convention Federalists (1814–15) similarly protested federal war policy as unconstitutional overreach and asserted states' rights — the same sectional-protest vocabulary Calhoun deployed for nullification.

                                                                  • A: Jackson's supporters denouncing the 'corrupt bargain' of 1824 were attacking an allegedly stolen election — a democratic-populist complaint about elite dealmaking, not a constitutional theory of state protest against federal overreach.
                                                                  • B: Correct. The New England Federalists at the Hartford Convention (1814–15) protested the War of 1812 and the embargo as unconstitutional federal overreach, asserted states' rights, and even flirted with nullification — the same sectional-protest vocabulary Calhoun would deploy for South Carolina against the tariff. Calhoun's 'protest' echoes the Federalists' protest a generation earlier.
                                                                  • C: The Jefferson administration's confrontation with the Barbary pirates was a foreign-policy naval action, not a states'-rights protest against federal overreach. It shares no language with Calhoun's constitutional argument.
                                                                  • D: Shays's rebels protested Massachusetts fiscal policy — taxes and debt collection — with armed uprising, not with constitutional theories of state sovereignty against federal power. Their vocabulary was debt and courts, not nullification.
