                                                                  [Image description: Carey Orr, 'The Trojan Horse at Our Gate,' September 17, 1935 — a conservative cartoon portraying New Deal programs as a deceptive threat to American liberty.] The cartoon's point is which of the following?

                                                                  1. A The New Deal's immigration proposals would endanger American democracy.
                                                                  2. B The New Deal could not solve the problems of the Great Depression.
                                                                  3. C The Supreme Court behaved tyrannically in striking down New Deal laws.
                                                                  4. D New Deal programs smuggled unconstitutional restrictions on freedoms.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: D

                                                                  Orr's 1935 cartoon — a Trojan horse labeled with New Deal agencies wheeled toward a walled city of liberty — charged that Roosevelt's programs, however benign their packaging, carried unconstitutional federal coercion inside.

                                                                  • A: The New Deal's immigration proposals are not the cartoon's subject — Orr's 1935 Trojan horse is labeled with New Deal agencies and aimed at a walled city of liberty. Immigration has nothing to do with it.
                                                                  • B: The cartoon does not argue the New Deal failed to end the Depression — its charge is constitutional, not economic. Whether the programs worked is beside the point; the claim is that they smuggled federal coercion past American liberty.
                                                                  • C: Orr's cartoon is conservative — it agrees with the Court's suspicion of the New Deal. It would not depict the justices who struck down New Deal laws as tyrannical; the 'threat' in the image is Roosevelt's programs, not the Court.
                                                                  • D: Correct. Orr's 1935 cartoon shows a Trojan horse labeled with New Deal agencies being wheeled toward a walled city of liberty: the charge that Roosevelt's programs, however benign their packaging — relief, recovery, reform — carried unconstitutional federal coercion inside, smuggling restrictions on American freedoms past the gates.

                                                                  The New Deal fight — whether Washington may manage the economy through agencies, codes, and spending — is the twentieth century's sharpest episode of the permanent American debate over government's economic role.

                                                                  • A: Correct. The New Deal fight — whether Washington may manage the economy through agencies, codes, and spending — is the twentieth century's sharpest episode of the permanent American debate over the federal government's role in the economy. The cartoon's anti-statist sentiment is one side of that enduring argument, recurring from the Grange and Populists through the Great Society to the present.
                                                                  • B: The cartoon does not complain about the Supreme Court legislating from the bench — in 1935 the conservative Court was the New Deal's enemy, not its ally.                                                                   • C: Federal versus state authority is adjacent but not the cartoon's core: Orr's target is federal power over the economy and individual liberty as such, not the division of power between Washington and the states.
                                                                  • D: Individual liberties in wartime — the classic civil-liberties-in-crisis debate — is not this cartoon's subject. Its liberties are economic: freedom from federal management of business, agriculture, and labor in peacetime.

                                                                  QA findings

                                                                  • No findings
                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-30

                                                                  The conflict over the Pennsylvania law reflected which fact about the Constitution's framers?

                                                                  1. A They explicitly protected slavery 'in perpetuity' in the original states.
                                                                  2. B They let states opt out of federal laws conflicting with state constitutions.
                                                                  3. C They postponed resolving the problem of slavery.
                                                                  4. D They declared enslaved people to be simultaneously citizens and property.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: C

                                                                  The framers' compromises — the fugitive-slave clause, the three-fifths clause, the 1808 slave-trade clause — deferred the slavery question; personal-liberty laws vs. fugitive-slave enforcement were the deferred crisis erupting.

                                                                  • A: The framers did not protect slavery 'in perpetuity' — the Constitution allowed Congress to end the slave trade after 1808, which it did. The compromises protected slavery for a time, not forever.
                                                                  • B: The framers allowed no such opt-out — the Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme over conflicting state law. States could not simply decline federal laws that clashed with their constitutions; that was the whole point of replacing the Articles.
                                                                  • C: Correct. The framers' compromises — the fugitive-slave clause, the three-fifths clause, the 1808 slave-trade clause — deferred the slavery question rather than resolving it. The collision between Pennsylvania's personal-liberty laws and federal fugitive-slave enforcement was the deferred crisis erupting: the Constitution had papered over slavery, and the paper was tearing.
                                                                  • D: The framers declared no such paradox. The Constitution never called enslaved people citizens — Dred Scott would later make explicit that they were not — and it avoided the word 'slavery' altogether, speaking of 'persons held to service.' The document evaded the question; it did not declare a contradiction.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-31

                                                                  Dix's campaign of memorials like this one most directly led to which of the following?

                                                                  1. A The creation of state mental asylums and the reform of existing insane asylums.
                                                                  2. B The granting of women's suffrage.
                                                                  3. C The immediate abolition of slavery.
                                                                  4. D The passage of national prohibition.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: A

                                                                  Dix's graphic memorials — describing the insane 'in cages, closets, cellars, stalls, pens! Chained, naked, beaten with rods' — were presented legislature by legislature to shame lawmakers into action, and they worked: her campaign directly produced new state asylums and the reform of brutal existing institutions across the country.

                                                                  • A: Correct. Dorothea Dix's graphic memorials — describing insane persons 'in cages, closets, cellars, stalls, pens! Chained, naked, beaten with rods' — were presented legislature by legislature to shame lawmakers into action, and they worked: her campaign directly produced new state mental asylums and the reform of brutal existing ones, beginning in Massachusetts and spreading across the country.
                                                                  • B: Women's suffrage was a different cause on a different timeline — Seneca Falls was 1848, but the vote took until 1920. Dix's memorials were about the treatment of the insane, not the franchise.
                                                                  • C: The immediate abolition of slavery was the abolitionists' demand, not Dix's. Her memorials addressed the insane poor, not enslaved people; the two reform causes shared the era but not the campaign.
                                                                  • D: National prohibition came seventy years later (the Eighteenth Amendment, 1919) from the temperance movement, not from Dix's asylum campaign. Her memorials never addressed alcohol.

                                                                  QA findings

                                                                  • major · answer_tell — keyed answer is uniquely and substantially longest
                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-32

                                                                  Dix's investigation and lobbying are best understood in the context of which development?

                                                                  1. A Women winning the vote in many states.
                                                                  2. B An economic depression closing state institutions.
                                                                  3. C A new federal role in health and poverty policy.
                                                                  4. D The rise of voluntary reform associations.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: D

                                                                  Antebellum reform ran through voluntary benevolent societies — moral-reform, temperance, and asylum associations — through which (mostly middle-class, often female) reformers pressured legislatures, as Dix did in Massachusetts.

                                                                  • A: Women did not win the vote in many states in the 1840s — only Wyoming Territory (1869) broke the barrier, decades later. Dix's lobbying succeeded without any electoral leverage from women's suffrage.
                                                                  • B: No economic depression was closing state institutions in this period — the 1840s saw institution-building, not retrenchment. Dix's context was reformers demanding more and better asylums, not defending them against budget cuts.
                                                                  • C: There was no federal role in health and poverty policy in the 1840s — Dix's one attempt at federal action, the 1854 land-grant bill for asylums, was vetoed by President Pierce on states'-rights grounds. Her campaign worked state by state precisely because Washington was absent.
                                                                  • D: Correct. Antebellum reform ran through voluntary benevolent associations — moral-reform, temperance, and asylum societies — through which mostly middle-class, often female reformers investigated conditions and pressured legislatures. Dix's memorial campaign is the classic case: a private citizen's investigation turned into legislative leverage, the voluntary-association method in action.

                                                                  • No findings
                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-35

                                                                  The song and its movement highlight which broader late-1800s development?

                                                                  1. A Popular outrage at the government-business alliance, driving demands for democratic reform.
                                                                  2. B A mass farmer-worker coalition that came to dominate federal legislation.
                                                                  3. C The collapse of the two-party system and the rise of a new major party that quickly won Congress.
                                                                  4. D Frontier warfare with Native peoples that embittered western farmers.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: A

                                                                  The Populist revolt was fueled by the perception that railroads, banks, and trusts had captured government — the same anger that drove the Granger, Populist, and then Progressive pushes for direct election of senators, the income tax, and antitrust action.

                                                                  • A: Correct. The song and its movement highlight the late-1800s perception that railroads, banks, and trusts had captured government — 'monopolies banded together' with 'old party bosses.' That popular outrage at the government-business alliance drove the era's demands for democratic reform: direct election of senators, the income tax, antitrust action, carried from the Grangers through the Populists to the Progressives.
                                                                  • B: No farmer-worker coalition dominated federal legislation in this era — the Populists tried to build one and failed (notably in 1896), and Congress remained in the hands of the two major parties. The movement's significance was as pressure, not as ruler.
                                                                  • C: The two-party system did not collapse, and no new major party won Congress. The People's Party peaked as a third party and then faded into the Democrats after 1896; the Republicans and Democrats kept their duopoly.
                                                                  • D: Frontier warfare with Native peoples is not the song's subject and did not drive this movement. The 'hayseed's' enemies are railroads and monopolies, not the U.S. Army's Indian wars.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-37

                                                                  Garvey's position belongs to which ongoing American debate?

                                                                  1. A Interventionism versus isolationism in foreign policy.
                                                                  2. B Separatism versus integration for African Americans.
                                                                  3. C Exclusion versus inclusion in immigration policy.
                                                                  4. D Laissez-faire versus government intervention in the economy.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: B

                                                                  Garvey's nationalism vs. the NAACP's integrationism is the classic form of the enduring Black freedom-struggle debate: build separate Black institutions and nationhood, or fight for full inclusion in American institutions.

                                                                  • A: Interventionism versus isolationism is a foreign-policy debate; Garvey's position was about Black identity and destiny, not about America's role in the world.
                                                                  • B: Correct. Garvey's nationalism versus the NAACP's integrationism is the classic form of the enduring debate within the Black freedom struggle: build separate Black institutions and claim separate nationhood, or fight for full inclusion and equality within American institutions. It runs from Washington and Du Bois through Garvey to the Nation of Islam and the integrationist civil-rights movement.
                                                                  • C: Exclusion versus inclusion in immigration policy is a different debate about who may enter the country. Garvey's question was about Black people's relationship to American society, not about immigration law.
                                                                  • D: Laissez-faire versus government intervention is an economic-policy debate. Garvey's nationalism was about race, identity, and nationhood — not about the government's role in the economy.

                                                                  • No findings
                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-38

                                                                  According to Gilmore, Black women's progressivism stayed 'nearly invisible' in histories mainly because of which of the following?

                                                                  1. A Their work left few written documents, since they organized without money, political protection, or publicity.
                                                                  2. B Black women's activism began only after the 1920s.
                                                                  3. C Black women generally opposed the Progressive movement's goals.
                                                                  4. D White progressives carefully documented Black women's contributions.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: A

                                                                  Gilmore's point is archival: Black women 'took up every reform white women pursued, reshaped progressivism from below, and built networks of Black activists, all without money, political protection, or publicity.' Because their work left few documents, historians working from the paper trail wrote them out — an absence of sources, not an absence of activism.

                                                                  • A: Correct. Gilmore's point is archival: Black women 'took up every reform white women pursued, reshaped progressivism from below, and built networks of Black activists, all without money, political protection, or publicity.' Because their work left few written documents, historians working from the paper trail wrote them out — invisibility produced not by absence of activism but by absence of archives.
                                                                  • B: Black women's activism in Gilmore's account runs from 1896 to 1920 — the Progressive Era itself, not something beginning after the 1920s. The chronology is the point: they were there all along, undocumented.
                                                                  • C: Black women did not oppose the Progressive movement's goals — they pursued them: temperance, moral reform, education, uplift. Their work paralleled white women's reform agendas; what differed was the Jim Crow context that forced it underground.
                                                                  • D: White progressives did not carefully document Black women's contributions — that is precisely Gilmore's complaint. The white reform record largely ignored Black women's parallel work, which is why the histories went blind to it.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-44

                                                                  Which earlier or later colonial episode belongs to the same continuity as the Paxton march?

                                                                  1. A The expulsion of Anne Hutchinson from Massachusetts Bay.
                                                                  2. B Bacon's Rebellion in Virginia (1676).
                                                                  3. C The Boston Tea Party (1773).
                                                                  4. D The trial of John Peter Zenger (1735).
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: B

                                                                  Bacon's Rebellion (1676) — frontier Virginians rising against Governor Berkeley's elite over Indian policy and political exclusion — is the direct predecessor of the Paxton pattern: backcountry resentment of seaboard elites.

                                                                  • A: Anne Hutchinson's expulsion (1638) was about religious dissent in Massachusetts Bay — antinomian theology challenging the ministers' authority. It shares nothing with the Paxton pattern of backcountry violence against seaboard elites over Indian policy.
                                                                  • B: Correct. Bacon's Rebellion (1676) — frontier Virginians rising against Governor Berkeley's elite over Indian policy and political exclusion — is the direct predecessor of the Paxton pattern: backcountry resentment of seaboard elites who monopolized power while leaving the frontier exposed. Same grievance, same social geography, a century apart.
                                                                  • C: The Boston Tea Party (1773) was an urban protest against Parliamentary taxation — a seaport crowd defying imperial authority, not backcountry settlers defying their own colonial elite over Indian policy.
                                                                  • D: The Zenger trial (1735) was about freedom of the press in New York — a printer acquitted of seditious libel. It belongs to the history of civil liberties, not to frontier-elite conflict.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-45

                                                                  The Port Huron Statement was drafted by which of the following groups?

                                                                  1. A The American Federation of Labor.
                                                                  2. B The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC).
                                                                  3. C The Young Americans for Freedom.
                                                                  4. D Students for a Democratic Society (SDS).
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: D

                                                                  The 1962 Port Huron Statement — written by young activists moved 'from silence to activism' by Southern racism and the Bomb — was the founding manifesto of Students for a Democratic Society, the organization that would anchor the student New Left through the decade.

                                                                  • A: The American Federation of Labor was the established trade-union federation — bureaucratic, older, and uninterested in student manifestos. The Port Huron Statement was written by young radicals, not by labor's leadership.
                                                                  • B: SNCC — the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee — was the civil-rights student organization, focused on Southern voter registration and desegregation. It shared the decade's activism but was a different organization with a different mission.
                                                                  • C: Young Americans for Freedom was the conservative youth organization, founded in 1960 at Sharon, Connecticut — the right's answer to the student left. The Port Huron Statement's critique of the Cold War and racial bigotry was the opposite of YAF's politics.
                                                                  • D: Correct. The 1962 Port Huron Statement — written by young activists moved 'from silence to activism' by Southern racism and the Bomb — was the founding manifesto of Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), the organization that would anchor the student New Left through the 1960s.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-46

                                                                  The statement's outlook repudiates which Eisenhower-era policy?

                                                                  1. A The 'New Look' defense policy built around nuclear weapons.
                                                                  2. B Increased funding for the United Nations.
                                                                  3. C Federal intervention in the Little Rock, Arkansas school-desegregation crisis.
                                                                  4. D The renewed federal emphasis on education.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: A

                                                                  The statement's horror at 'the Bomb' and the Cold War system directly rejects Eisenhower's New Look — deterrence through massive nuclear retaliation ('more bang for the buck') — which made nuclear annihilation the centerpiece of American strategy.

                                                                  • A: Correct. The statement's horror at 'the Bomb' and the Cold War system directly rejects Eisenhower's 'New Look' defense policy — deterrence built around massive nuclear retaliation, 'more bang for the buck,' which made the threat of nuclear annihilation the centerpiece of American strategy. The Port Huron generation found that bargain morally intolerable.
                                                                  • B: The statement did not repudiate funding for the United Nations — if anything, SDS's internationalism was sympathetic to world institutions. The UN was not Eisenhower's controversial policy; the Bomb was.
                                                                  • C: Federal intervention at Little Rock (1957) enforced school desegregation — a use of federal power the New Left supported, not repudiated. The statement's authors were moved to activism by Southern racism; they would not condemn the troops who protected Black students.
                                                                  • D: The renewed federal emphasis on education (the National Defense Education Act, 1958) expanded the very universities SDS recruited from. The statement did not repudiate education funding; it repudiated the nuclear-centered Cold War.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-47

                                                                  The statement was primarily addressed to which audience?

                                                                  1. A Southern Black Americans.
                                                                  2. B Federal government officials in Washington, D.C.
                                                                  3. C Middle-class college students.
                                                                  4. D Industrial factory workers.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: C

                                                                  SDS wrote for its own constituency: the expanding, largely middle-class student population of 1960s universities — 'we are people of this generation' — not workers, officials, or Southern Black activists.

                                                                  • A: The statement was not addressed to Southern Black Americans — SDS wrote as allies of the civil-rights movement, not as its voice. The 'we' of Port Huron is the student generation speaking to itself.
                                                                  • B: The statement was not addressed to federal officials — it was a manifesto of a student movement, not a lobbying document. Its audience was generational, not governmental.
                                                                  • C: Correct. SDS wrote for its own constituency: the expanding, largely middle-class student population of 1960s universities — 'we are people of this generation,' raised in 'modest comfort' and now confronting the gap between American ideals and American realities. The statement is students addressing students.
                                                                  • D: Industrial factory workers were not the audience — SDS was a student organization, and its famous later turn toward workers (the 1969 'worker-student alliance' debates) came years after Port Huron. In 1962 the audience was the campus.

                                                                  QA findings

                                                                  • No findings
                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-48

                                                                  SDS's growth through the 1960s is best understood in the context of which of the following?

                                                                  1. A Rapid industrialization and urban congestion.
                                                                  2. B The baby boom, postwar prosperity, and expanding education.
                                                                  3. C Economic polarization and supply-side policy.
                                                                  4. D Personal computers, the religious right, and student apathy.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: B

                                                                  The New Left was a creature of affluence and demography: baby-boom cohorts flooding newly expanded universities, with the security to critique the very system that produced their comfort.

                                                                  • A: Rapid industrialization and urban congestion describe the turn of the twentieth century — the world of the Progressives and the early labor movement, not the student New Left of the 1960s.
                                                                  • B: Correct. SDS's growth is inseparable from demography and affluence: the baby boom flooding newly expanded universities, postwar prosperity giving middle-class youth the security to critique the system that produced their comfort. The New Left was a creature of abundance — students with full stomachs and uneasy consciences.
                                                                  • C: Economic polarization and supply-side policy belong to the 1980s — Reagan's era, after SDS had collapsed. They explain the right's ascendancy, not the student left's rise.
                                                                  • D: Personal computers, the religious right, and student apathy are 1980s–90s phenomena. SDS grew in the early-mid 1960s, in the world of the Bomb, civil rights, and campus expansion — not the world of the PC and the Moral Majority.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-51

                                                                  The act's concerns most directly reflect which continuity in American history?

                                                                  1. A Continuing debates over voting rights.
                                                                  2. B Continuing debates over federal power in marriage law.
                                                                  3. C Continuing debates over employment discrimination.
                                                                  4. D Continuing debates over the legal status of women.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: D

                                                                  From feme covert to Seneca Falls to suffrage to the ERA fight, the legal personhood of women — property, contract, citizenship — is one of American history's longest continuities.

                                                                  • A: Voting rights are a different continuity — the franchise fights from Jacksonian democracy through the Fifteenth and Nineteenth Amendments. The property act was about wives' legal personhood: owning, inheriting, and conveying property.
                                                                  • B: Federal power in marriage law was not the issue — marriage law was and remains state law, and the 1848 act was a New York statute. The continuity is about women's status, not federalism.
                                                                  • C: Employment discrimination is a twentieth-century continuity (Title VII, 1964). The 1848 act concerned property and contract rights within marriage, not workplace equality.
                                                                  • D: Correct. From feme covert — the common-law doctrine that a wife's legal identity merged into her husband's — through Seneca Falls, suffrage, and the ERA fight, the legal personhood of women (property, contract, citizenship) is one of American history's longest continuities. The 1848 act was an early landmark in it.

                                                                  • No findings
                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-53

                                                                  Which constitutional provision most fully enshrined the Remonstrance's principle in American law?

                                                                  1. A The Declaration of Independence's preamble.
                                                                  2. B The Constitution's enumeration of congressional powers.
                                                                  3. C The First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause.
                                                                  4. D The First Amendment's Establishment Clause.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: C

                                                                  The Remonstrance defends the free practice of religion against government coercion — the principle the Free Exercise Clause ('Congress shall make no law... prohibiting the free exercise thereof') constitutionalized in 1791.

                                                                  • A: The Declaration's preamble ('life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness') is a statement of revolutionary principles, not constitutional law — it enshrined nothing enforceable. The Remonstrance's principle became law through the Bill of Rights, not the Declaration.
                                                                  • B: The enumeration of congressional powers defines what the federal government may do — it is about the scope of federal authority, not about religious liberty. The Remonstrance's principle needed a rights provision, not a powers list.
                                                                  • C: Correct. The Remonstrance defends the free practice of religion against government coercion — townspeople insisting they cannot in conscience persecute Quakers for worshipping. That principle was constitutionalized in 1791 in the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause: 'Congress shall make no law... prohibiting the free exercise thereof.'
                                                                  • D: The Establishment Clause ('Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion') bars government from setting up or favoring a church — the other half of the religion clauses. The Remonstrance is about the freedom to practice one's faith without persecution, which is free exercise, not disestablishment.

                                                                  MCQbarrons-2027-pt1-55

                                                                  Cuffe's petition best illustrates which development?

                                                                  1. A Revolutionary rhetoric inspired marginalized groups to demand inclusion.
                                                                  2. B Slave revolts like Stono inspired widespread imitation across North America.
                                                                  3. C Black Loyalists felt doubly vulnerable after Britain's defeat.
                                                                  4. D Massachusetts treated Black residents worse than British colonial rule had.
                                                                  Answer and explanation

                                                                  Key: A

                                                                  The petition is a classic case of the Revolution's egalitarian language escaping its authors' control: 'no taxation without representation' became a weapon for free Black Northerners demanding the franchise.

                                                                  • A: Correct. Cuffe's petition is a classic case of the Revolution's egalitarian language escaping its authors' control: 'no taxation without representation' — coined against Parliament — became a weapon for free Black Northerners demanding the franchise from Massachusetts. Revolutionary rhetoric inspired marginalized groups to turn the Revolution's principles against the Revolution's limits.
                                                                  • B: The Stono Rebellion (1739) was a slave uprising in South Carolina, decades before the Revolution and unrelated to Cuffe's petition. The petition illustrates rhetoric inspiring demands for inclusion, not revolts inspiring imitation.
                                                                  • C: Black Loyalists — enslaved people who fled to British lines during the war — are a different story from Cuffe, a free Black Massachusetts mariner and merchant petitioning the state government after independence. His petition is about the Revolution's promises, not Loyalist vulnerability.
                                                                  • D: Massachusetts did not treat Black residents worse than British colonial rule had — the petition itself proves the opposite: Cuffe could appeal to revolutionary principles and petition the legislature, a political avenue British rule never offered. His argument assumes the Revolution's ideals are real and binding.

                                                                              DBQbarrons-2027-pt2-dbq

                                                                              Americans debated and addressed immigration policy in the period 1754–1800 and again in the period 1875–1925. Evaluate the extent to which the ways they debated and addressed immigration changed between the two periods.

                                                                                Documents
                                                                                1. Document 1: Benjamin Franklin, Observations Concerning the Increase of Mankind, Peopling of Countries, etc. (written 1751; published 1755).

                                                                                  Why should the [Germans] be suffered to swarm into our Settlements, and by herding together establish their Language and Manners to the Exclusion of ours? Why should Pennsylvania, founded by the English, become a Colony of Aliens, who will shortly be so numerous as to Germanize us instead of our Anglifying them, and will never adopt our Language or Customs, any more than they can acquire our Complexion.

                                                                                2. Document 2: J. Hector St. John de Crevecoeur, Letters From an American Farmer, Letter III (1782).

                                                                                  What then is the American, this new man? He is either an European, or the descendant of an European, hence that strange mixture of blood, which you will find in no other country. I could point out to you a family whose grandfather was an Englishman, whose wife was Dutch, whose son married a French woman, and whose present four sons have now four wives of different nations. He is an American, who leaving behind him all his ancient prejudices and manners, receives new ones from the new mode of life he has embraced, the new government he obeys, and the new rank he holds. He becomes an American by being received in the broad lap of our great Alma Mater. Here individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men, whose labours and posterity will one day cause great changes in the world.

                                                                                3. Document 3: Theodore Sedgwick, from debate in the House of Representatives over the Naturalization Bill, 1794.

                                                                                  And shall we alone adopt the rash theory that the subjects of all governments despotic, monarchical, and aristocratical are, as soon as they set foot on American ground, qualified to participate in administering the sovereignty of our country? Shall we hold the benefits of American citizenship so cheap as to invite, nay, almost bribe, the discontented, the ambitious, and the avaricious of every country to accept them? . . . A war, the most cruel and dreadful which has been known for centuries, was now raging in those in all those countries from which emigrants were to be expected. . . . Could any reasonable man believe, that men who, actuated by such passions, had fought on grounds so opposite, almost equally distant from the happy mean we had chosen, would here mingle in social affections with each other, or with us?

                                                                                4. Document 4: Joseph McDonnell, Labor Standard, June 30, 1878.

                                                                                  The cry that the 'Chinese must go' is both narrow and unjust. It represents no broad or universal principle. It is merely a repetition of the cry that was raised years ago by American Indians against the immigration of Irishmen, Englishmen, Germans and others from European nations. It now ill becomes those, or the descendants of those, against whom this cry was raised in past years, to raise a similar tocsin against a class of foreigners who have been degraded by ages of oppression. . . . The feeling at the bottom of the 'Know Nothing' movement IN ITS EARLY DAYS was certainly a general one against low wages, and if it had raised the cry: No low wages. No cheap labor! Instead of sounding the intolerant, silly, and shameful cry against Irishmen, Englishmen, Germans and all other 'foreigners,' it would have accomplished incalculable good.

                                                                                5. Document 5: Joseph Keppler, 'Welcome to All!' Puck, 1880.

                                                                                  [Image description: Joseph Keppler's 1880 cartoon presents the United States as a great ark afloat on rough seas, taking immigrant families of many nations aboard while dark storm clouds mass over Europe behind them — America pictured as a haven from Old World turmoil, open to all.]

                                                                                6. Document 6: Madison Grant, The Passing of the Great Race (1916).

                                                                                  These new immigrants were no longer exclusively members of the Nordic race as were the earlier ones who came of their own impulse to improve their social conditions. The transportation lines advertised America as a land flowing with milk and honey, and the European governments took the opportunity to unload upon careless, wealthy, and hospitable America the sweepings of their jails and asylums. The result was that the new immigration, while it still included many strong elements from the north of Europe, contained a large and increasing number of the weak, the broken, and the mentally crippled of all races drawn from the lowest stratum of the Mediterranean basin and the Balkans, together with hordes of the wretched, submerged populations of the Polish Ghettos.

                                                                                7. Document 7: Frank Beard, 'Columbia's Unwelcome Guests,' 1885.

                                                                                  [Image description: Frank Beard's 1885 cartoon shows the female figure of Columbia recoiling as a crowd of 'unwelcome guests' presses in on her; behind them, vermin stream from drains marked with the names of Italy, Russia, and Germany, while the arriving figures are tagged as anarchists, socialists, and members of the Mafia — a warning against unrestricted immigration.]

                                                                                Answer and explanation

                                                                                Key: —

                                                                                In both 1750–1800 and 1875–1925, Americans fiercely contested who could become American — nativists warning of cultural dilution (Docs 1, 6, 7) against defenders of an expansive, welcoming nation (Docs 2, 4, 5) — but the debate changed fundamentally: the early argument turned on cultural assimilation and political loyalty to a fragile republic, while the later argument absorbed industrial-era fears of low wages and unemployment plus a new racial 'science' of immutable inferiority, producing far more sweeping federal restrictions, from Chinese exclusion to the 1920s quota system. Change outweighs continuity in tone, scale, and consequence.

                                                                                  QA findings

                                                                                  • No findings
                                                                                  LEQbarrons-2027-pt2-leq

                                                                                  From the French and Indian War through the Civil War, Britain's North American colonies and then the United States fought a series of military conflicts. Explain how participation in these conflicts influenced American national identity in the period from 1754 to 1877.

                                                                                    Answer and explanation

                                                                                    Key: —

                                                                                    The French and Indian War and the American Revolution began transforming colonial identity: British victory removed the French threat and then Britain's postwar taxes and restrictions made many colonists question their allegiance, so that by 1776 a growing number thought of themselves as Americans rather than Britons — though a substantial Loyalist minority did not. The Civil War completed the transformation in a different key: it forged the 'United States' as a singular nation rather than a compact of states, and emancipation recast the national experiment as a test of whether the Declaration's promise of equality could be made real.

                                                                                      MCQbarrons-2027-pt2-03

                                                                                      This cartoonist would most likely have condemned which of the following?

                                                                                      1. A The McCarran Internal Security Act, passed over Truman's veto
                                                                                      2. B Eisenhower's 1961 warning about the 'military-industrial complex'
                                                                                      3. C Nixon's 1959 'Kitchen Debate' with Khrushchev
                                                                                      4. D The Truman Doctrine, which committed the United States to containing Soviet expansion abroad
                                                                                      Answer and explanation

                                                                                      Key: A

                                                                                      The cartoonist attacked the anti-Communist overreaction, so he would have condemned the McCarran Internal Security Act (1950) — Congress's loyalty-security crackdown passed over Truman's veto — not containment abroad or Eisenhower's warning against militarism.

                                                                                      • A: Correct. The cartoonist attacked the anti-Communist overreaction at home, so he would have condemned the McCarran Internal Security Act (1950) — Congress's loyalty-security crackdown, requiring Communist organizations to register and authorizing detention of suspected subversives, passed over Truman's veto. It was exactly the kind of liberty-endangering panic the cartoon depicts.
                                                                                      • B: Eisenhower's 1961 farewell warning about the 'military-industrial complex' cautioned against militarism and the arms industry's influence — a skepticism of power that aligns with, rather than offends, the cartoonist's civil-libertarian outlook.
                                                                                      • C: Nixon's 1959 'Kitchen Debate' with Khrushchev was Cold War propaganda theater about consumer capitalism versus Communism — a foreign-policy exchange, not a domestic repression measure. The cartoonist's quarrel was with the domestic crackdown, not with debating Khrushchev.
                                                                                      • D: The Truman Doctrine committed the United States to containing Soviet expansion abroad — the cartoonist's target was the domestic overreaction (loyalty programs, blacklists), not the foreign policy of containment. Herblock supported containing Communism; he opposed the panic at home.

                                                                                      QA findings

                                                                                      • No findings
                                                                                      MCQbarrons-2027-pt2-04

                                                                                      Franklin's argument in this passage anticipates which later American principle?

                                                                                      1. A 'No taxation without representation.'
                                                                                      2. B The Monroe Doctrine's warning to European powers.
                                                                                      3. C Judicial review of acts of Congress.
                                                                                      4. D The two-term tradition for presidents.
                                                                                      Answer and explanation

                                                                                      Key: A

                                                                                      Franklin concedes Parliament may lay 'external' duties regulating commerce but insists colonists 'could not be taxed by a Parliament wherein we were not represented.' The underlying principle — that legitimate taxation requires the taxpayers' representation — became the Revolution's rallying cry: no taxation without representation.

                                                                                      • A: Correct. Franklin concedes that Parliament may lay 'external' duties regulating commerce, but insists colonists 'could not be taxed by a Parliament wherein we were not represented.' The underlying principle — that legitimate taxation requires the taxpayers' representation — became the Revolution's rallying cry: no taxation without representation.
                                                                                      • B: The Monroe Doctrine (1823) warned Europe against new colonization in the Americas — a foreign-policy doctrine with nothing to do with Franklin's argument about taxation and representation.
                                                                                      • C: Judicial review of acts of Congress (Marbury v. Madison, 1803) is about the courts' power over legislation, not about the colonists' claim against parliamentary taxation. Different principle, different century.
                                                                                      • D: The two-term presidential tradition came from Washington's retirement, not from Franklin's tax argument. It has no connection to representation and revenue.

                                                                                      QA findings

                                                                                      • No findings
                                                                                      MCQbarrons-2027-pt2-06

                                                                                      Which colonial action best embodied Franklin's reasoning in the passage?

                                                                                      1. A Anti-Federalist demands for adding a Bill of Rights to the Constitution during ratification
                                                                                      2. B The Stamp Act Congress's 1765 petition protesting parliamentary taxation
                                                                                      3. C South Carolina's nullification of the tariff in 1832
                                                                                      4. D The probusiness policies of Coolidge and Hoover in the 1920s
                                                                                      Answer and explanation

                                                                                      Key: B

                                                                                      The Stamp Act Congress (1765) petitioned against parliamentary taxation using exactly Franklin's logic — external commercial duties were tolerable, internal taxes without representation were not — making it the direct institutional expression of his argument.

                                                                                      • A: The Anti-Federalists' demand for a Bill of Rights during ratification (1787–88) was about limiting the new federal government's power over individuals — a constitutional-design debate, not an application of Franklin's tax logic about Parliament.
                                                                                      • B: Correct. The Stamp Act Congress (1765) petitioned against parliamentary taxation using exactly Franklin's distinction: external duties regulating commerce were tolerable, but internal taxes laid without colonial representation were not. It was the direct institutional expression of his argument — the colonies' first united constitutional protest.
                                                                                      • C: South Carolina's nullification of the tariff (1832) was a states'-rights claim that a state could void a federal law — a different constitutional theory (nullification) applied to a different grievance (protective tariffs), decades later.
                                                                                      • D: The probusiness policies of Coolidge and Hoover in the 1920s — tax cuts, regulatory restraint — belong to a different century and a different debate entirely, with no connection to Franklin's reasoning about representation.

                                                                                      • No findings
                                                                                      MCQbarrons-2027-pt2-09

                                                                                      Jackson's removal approach was most significantly revised by the

                                                                                      1. A Homestead Act of 1862
                                                                                      2. B Immigration Act of 1921
                                                                                      3. C Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
                                                                                      4. D Dawes Act of 1887
                                                                                      Answer and explanation

                                                                                      Key: D

                                                                                      The Dawes Act (1887) reversed removal's premise: instead of segregating tribes on distant reservations, it broke up tribal landholding into individual allotments to force assimilation — a fundamental alteration of Jackson-era policy.

                                                                                      • A: The Homestead Act (1862) gave western public land to settlers — it accelerated the pressure on Native lands rather than revising the removal policy's logic. It was about settling the West, not about rethinking Indian policy.
                                                                                      • B: The Immigration Act of 1921 restricted European immigration through quotas — entirely unrelated to Native American removal policy.
                                                                                      • C: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) constitutionalized racial segregation — a different policy domain (Jim Crow) with no bearing on the federal government's approach to tribal lands.
                                                                                      • D: Correct. The Dawes Act (1887) fundamentally revised Jackson-era policy: instead of segregating tribes on distant reservations (removal's premise), it broke tribal landholding into individual allotments to force assimilation — dissolving the tribal land base rather than preserving it at a distance. Separation gave way to absorption.

                                                                                      QA findings

                                                                                      • No findings
                                                                                      MCQbarrons-2027-pt2-11

                                                                                      The segregation King opposed rested primarily on which Supreme Court decision?

                                                                                      1. A Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)
                                                                                      2. B Brown v. Board of Education (1954)
                                                                                      3. C Worcester v. Georgia (1832)
                                                                                      4. D Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
                                                                                      Answer and explanation

                                                                                      Key: D

                                                                                      Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) constitutionalized 'separate but equal,' giving Jim Crow segregation the Supreme Court's blessing that Brown (1954) later overturned.

                                                                                      • A: Dred Scott (1857) denied Black citizenship — a different legal foundation from segregation. The Jim Crow system King fought rested on 'separate but equal,' not on the denial of citizenship.
                                                                                      • B: Brown v. Board (1954) overturned segregation — it was the decision that undermined the system King opposed, not the one that sustained it.
                                                                                      • C: Worcester v. Georgia (1832) concerned Cherokee tribal sovereignty against Georgia — nothing to do with the segregation of public facilities.
                                                                                      • D: Correct. Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) constitutionalized 'separate but equal,' giving Jim Crow segregation the Supreme Court's blessing — the legal foundation of the segregated Birmingham King was demonstrating against, until Brown (1954) began its overturning.

                                                                                      MCQbarrons-2027-pt2-19

                                                                                      Which of the following was NOT intended to give government power over the industrialists' wealth?

                                                                                      1. A Sherman Anti-Trust Act (1890)
                                                                                      2. B Interstate Commerce Act (1887)
                                                                                      3. C Federal Trade Commission Act (1914)
                                                                                      4. D Newlands Reclamation Act (1902)
                                                                                      Answer and explanation

                                                                                      Key: D

                                                                                      The Sherman Act, Interstate Commerce Act, and FTC Act all targeted corporate power; the Newlands Reclamation Act (1902) funded western irrigation projects — conservation and development, not industrial regulation.

                                                                                      • A: The Sherman Anti-Trust Act (1890) was intended to give the government power over industrialists' wealth — it outlawed combinations in restraint of trade. Whatever its early enforcement failures, its purpose was corporate restraint.
                                                                                      • B: The Interstate Commerce Act (1887) created the ICC to regulate railroad rates and practices — a direct assertion of federal power over corporate wealth's transportation engine.
                                                                                      • C: The Federal Trade Commission Act (1914) created the FTC to police unfair business practices — again, government power aimed at corporate conduct.
                                                                                      • D: Correct. The Newlands Reclamation Act (1902) funded western irrigation projects with public-land sale revenues — a conservation and development measure to make arid lands farmable. It had nothing to do with regulating industrialists' wealth; it was about water in the West, not trusts in the East.

                                                                                      MCQbarrons-2027-pt2-22

                                                                                      The Fourteenth Amendment addressed the conditions Thomas describes by

                                                                                      1. A stripping voting rights from former Confederates.
                                                                                      2. B granting citizenship and equal protection of the laws to formerly enslaved people.
                                                                                      3. C creating an expedited Supreme Court appeals process for civil-rights claims.
                                                                                      4. D guaranteeing formerly enslaved people the forty acres promised by General Sherman's field order.
                                                                                      Answer and explanation

                                                                                      Key: B

                                                                                      The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) made formerly enslaved people citizens and guaranteed 'equal protection of the laws' — the direct constitutional answer to the rightlessness Thomas describes.

                                                                                      • A: The Fourteenth Amendment's Section 3 disqualified some former Confederates from office, but it did not strip voting rights from former Confederates wholesale — and officeholding disqualification was not the amendment's answer to the rightlessness of freedpeople.
                                                                                      • B: Correct. The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) made formerly enslaved people citizens — 'all persons born or naturalized in the United States' — and guaranteed them 'equal protection of the laws.' That was the direct constitutional answer to the conditions the Bureau official describes: a people treated as possessing no rights at all were made rights-bearing citizens.
                                                                                      • C: The amendment created no expedited Supreme Court appeals process for civil-rights claims — enforcement came through Congress's Section 5 power and later statutes, not through a special appellate track.
                                                                                      • D: The 'forty acres' of Sherman's Field Order 15 was reversed by President Johnson, who returned the land to pardoned Confederates. The Fourteenth Amendment guaranteed citizenship and equal protection, not land — it never promised forty acres.

                                                                                      MCQbarrons-2027-pt2-24

                                                                                      The Democratic-Republicans' opposition to this act was best expressed in which of the following?

                                                                                      1. A The Hartford Convention.
                                                                                      2. B The Nullification Proclamation.
                                                                                      3. C The Monroe Doctrine.
                                                                                      4. D The Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions.
                                                                                      Answer and explanation

                                                                                      Key: D

                                                                                      The Alien Friends Act — empowering the president to deport aliens deemed 'dangerous to the peace and safety of the United States' — was the Federalists' weapon against French immigrants and Democratic-Republican sympathizers during the Quasi-War. Jefferson and Madison answered with the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions (1798–99), denouncing the Alien and Sedition Acts as unconstitutional federal overreach.

                                                                                      • A: The Hartford Convention (1814–15) was New England Federalists protesting the War of 1812 — a different party, a different law, a different generation. It was the Federalists' protest, not the Democratic-Republicans' answer to the Alien Act.
                                                                                      • B: The Nullification Proclamation (1832) was Jackson's response to South Carolina's nullification of the tariff — decades later and about a different crisis entirely.
                                                                                      • C: The Monroe Doctrine (1823) was a foreign-policy statement about European non-intervention in the Americas — nothing to do with the Democratic-Republicans' opposition to the Alien Friends Act.
                                                                                      • D: Correct. The Alien Friends Act — empowering the president to deport aliens deemed 'dangerous to the peace and safety of the United States' — was the Federalists' weapon against French immigrants and Democratic-Republican sympathizers during the Quasi-War. Jefferson and Madison answered with the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions (1798–99), protesting the Acts as unconstitutional federal overreach.

                                                                                      MCQbarrons-2027-pt2-26

                                                                                      The federal power exercised in the excerpt most resembles federal action during

                                                                                      1. A the Mexican-American War against Mexican Americans.
                                                                                      2. B the Red Scare that followed World War I.
                                                                                      3. C the aftermath of the 1930s sit-down strikes.
                                                                                      4. D the FBI's COINTELPRO surveillance of 1960s protest movements.
                                                                                      Answer and explanation

                                                                                      Key: B

                                                                                      Like the Alien Act's targeting of suspect foreigners, the post-WWI Red Scare brought Palmer Raids — warrantless roundups and deportations of suspected radicals — the closest parallel in federal suppression of perceived alien threats.

                                                                                      • A: Federal action against Mexican Americans during the Mexican-American War is not the parallel — the Alien Act targeted suspect foreigners for deportation on political grounds, a domestic-security panic, not wartime treatment of a neighboring population.
                                                                                      • B: Correct. Like the Alien Act's targeting of suspect foreigners, the post-World War I Red Scare brought the Palmer Raids — warrantless roundups and deportations of suspected radicals and immigrants. Both episodes show the federal government using deportation and detention against perceived alien threats in moments of national-security panic.
                                                                                      • C: The aftermath of the 1930s sit-down strikes was about labor relations — the government's response ran through the Wagner Act's protections, not through deporting suspect aliens. A different kind of federal action entirely.
                                                                                      • D: The FBI's COINTELPRO surveillance of 1960s protest movements was covert domestic spying on American citizens — a different method (secret surveillance rather than public deportation law) aimed at a different target (domestic dissenters rather than suspect aliens). The Palmer Raids' roundups and deportations are the closer parallel to the Alien Act.

                                                                                      The passage argues that women's changing social roles resulted primarily from which of the following?

                                                                                      1. A The ratification of the women's suffrage amendment.
                                                                                      2. B Federal propaganda campaigns during wartime.
                                                                                      3. C The invention of the automobile.
                                                                                      4. D Economic necessity forcing women out of the home and into business and public life.
                                                                                      Answer and explanation

                                                                                      Key: D

                                                                                      The passage's thesis is explicit: 'the only force which is strong enough to break down social convention is economic necessity.' Women eating in public restaurants — 'the absolutely new social phenomenon of women dining alone' — happened because economic necessity 'forced women out of the home and into the world of business,' not because of legislation, propaganda, or technology.

                                                                                      • A: The suffrage amendment (1920) was a political victory, not the force the passage describes. The passage's thesis is economic: 'the only force which is strong enough to break down social convention is economic necessity' — women dining alone in public because work had forced them 'out of the home and into the world of business.'
                                                                                      • B: Federal wartime propaganda campaigns (the World Wars' 'Rosie the Riveter' era) came later than this passage's 1920s-era observation, and the passage credits economic necessity, not government messaging, with the change.
                                                                                      • C: The automobile transformed courtship and mobility, but it is not the passage's answer. The author names the force explicitly — economic necessity forcing women into business and public life — not the car.
                                                                                      • D: Correct. The passage's thesis is explicit: 'the only force which is strong enough to break down social convention is economic necessity.' Women eating in public restaurants — 'the absolutely new social phenomenon of women dining alone' — happened because economic necessity had 'forced women out of the home and into the world of business,' annihilating the old convention that respectable women ate only in private.
